speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)

speechtext: He is not an officer of the Tost Office Department.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
He is an officer of this House acting under the instruction of the I Postmaster General. These hags commenced

arriving here on the 20th of September. Every day as they came in here they were emptied and the contents were franked and they were sent to the post office. The post office took them in, put the stamp of the post office on them and threw them out into the corridor and to-day there are 300 bags lying there, stamped by the post office, blocking up the corridor around the front of the post office, in the lobbies, and extending down towards the telegraph offices. Each one of these has been through the post office and has been stamped by the officers of the department, but owing to instructions to receive only so many bags a day so as to prevent as far as possible the sending of this literature to the country, the city post office can take only forty bags a day while tons and tons of matter are going in from different departments for transmission through the mails. If, as the leader of the opposition asked this morning, a commission is appointed we will be able to prove that from every department mountains of literature, put up by servants and paid for by the people of; this country are being sent. In one department last week there were six men sitting around a table putting up this blue-book upon the transcontinental railway and the speech of the right hon. the Prime Minister. They were folding them up and sending them out under a minister's frank, paid for by the people of this country, and because the postmaster would not allow our bags to be delivered to us from the post office, as it is our right to have them delivered, we have had to pay $32 of express and then we have been refused the right of admission for express parcels into the House. Is this not a grievance for the opposition ? And yet when it is brought to the attention of the Prime Minister he laughs at it as if to say : You, the leader of the opposition, and the gentlemen supporting you have no rights in this House ; you cannot have express parcels come here ; our officers, the sergeant-at-arms, the chief messenger and the Speaker have forbidden it and it cannot come in. The sergeant-at-arms told me last night that it could not be delivered. I made up my mind that it would be if I had to walk through the sergeant-at-arms, the chief messenger, the Speaker and, back of them all, the Postmaster General. These gentlemen, like the coon in the tree, came down this morning and gave orders to carry it in and it is there and this House is not going to rise until the Postmaster General gets these bags through his post office, so the sooner the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition come to an agreement the sooner this House will prorogue. It will not prorogue a day before the opposition are satisfied that every package of literature that is in these buildings will be sent out, not that it will be held by the Postmaster General, who said a few minutes ago that we would Mr. TAYLOR.
be here until after Christmas if we waited until this was all sent out. We know what he will do ; the moment the session is over, as soon as the gun is fired, the franking privilege will cease and the Postmaster General will order a bonfire to burn up this literature. We know that he is afraid, that the Prime Minister is afraid to have this literature go to the country ; they are afraid to have the people of this country enlightened on this enormity of the transcontinental railway. We know that. The Postmaster General said that the whole system is blocked on account of the use of these mail bags. If a fire happened and these 1,830 mail bags were burnt would that block the post office system of this country ? Altogether in the last six weeks only 1,830 bags of this literature have been sent from the 'Star' office addressed to me here and they have not been in my possession twenty-four hours until they were emptied, their contents franked, and handed to the post office here to take charge of them. I want to ask the Postmaster General now why a couple of hundred bags addressed to me have been held at the Ottawa city post office for the last eight or ten days ?
Where is that ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: In the city post office, because Mr. Speaker gave his instructions to the sergeant-at-arms, and he to the chief messenger not to allow the bags to come into this building.
You say there are a quantity of bags addressed to you in the lobby of the post office at Ottawa.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: They are held in the post office at Ottawa ; the men brought them up here but had to draw them back again by order of the Speaker through the sergeant-at-arms and the chief messenger. They are down there now and I went to the post office and asked the postmaster why they were not delivered.

The hon. gentleman asks me a question but he, himself gives the answer because he says the Speaker refused to permit these bags to enter the building. I must say that I have never for a moment taken the liberty of suggesting anything to the Speaker, who is responsible for the proper administration of the lobbies of this House, in respect to this matter. I have nothing whatever to do with the actions of either the Speaker or of the sergeant-at-arms or any other officer of this House.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. gentleman said a while ago that the city post office is to blame. This stuff came in addressed to me atl the House of Commons and why has it not been delivered ?
I do not carry it around.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The leader of the opposition brought this to the attention of the Prime Minister this morning and he paid no attention to it. Here are the bags addressed to me lying in the post office a week and not delivered. That is a/ nice state of affairs. One load was brought up here, but by orders of the officers of this House they were not admitted, and I am satisfied, I have that much confidence in the Speaker, that unless there was some intimation from the Postmaster General he would not of his own accord say :	Do not admit literature
addressed to Mr. Taylor into the precincts of this House.

My hon. friend is entirely in error ; there has been no interference of any kind on my part or on the part of any one else to prevent the delivery of this mail matter. The only difficulty has arisen because of the state of the lobbies and halls of this House. The Speaker himself, of his own motion decided, that it was better not to allow any further accumulations. I requested the Speaker, if he could, to place a room at the disposal of the hon. gentleman that there might be no such difficulty and he informed me that he had placed at his disposal the Railway Committee room, the largest available room in this building, which it is thought will greatly relieve the congestion.
But how much floor space is there in it ?

Three thousand square feet. That room is at his disposal if he desires to use it. I may say that the mail service between the city post office and the House of Commons post office is not under the control of the Postmaster General or of the Post Office Department, but is under the control of the postmaster of the House of Commons, who is an officer of this House and therefore if there were facilities to receive this matter here the hon. gentleman could have it delivered at once.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The Postmaster General makes a very pleasant speech, but what are the facts ? He says that he requested the Speaker to get rooms and the Speaker kindly placed at the disposal of the ' Star ' men the Railway Committee room upstairs. I immediately went to the messenger department to know if I could have the stuff moved up there, but they could not give me a man to do it. Then we offered to hire six men, but that offer was not accepted nor were we allowed to use the elevator.
At one o'clock, House took recess.
House resumed at three o'clock.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
When the House rose at one o'clock, I was trying, in my humble
way, to refute the charge brought against me by_the Postmaster General, when he said that I had in my possesssion an enormous quantity of mail bags, and that if I did not deliver them by Monday morning-and the hon. gentleman knew very well that I would not be here until five o'clock on Monday afternoon-that he would take forcible possession of them by law. I want to explain how these bags came to be in my possession. They came addresssed to me. The contents were taken out and franked, and, at the request of the postmaster of the House of Commons, instead of being carried into the post office and dumped on the floor there, they were put back into the mail bags. The postmaster took the bags into the post office, sorted out the contents, stamped them with, the post office stamp, filled the bags again, and sent them out into the corridor, where they have been the last two or three days. How am I responsible ? If I or any one else attempted to empty the bags and hand them over to the Postmaster General, the postmaster could have us arrested for tampering with His Majesty's mails. The Postmaster General charges me with improperly holding these bags when they were in the charge of the postmaster of this House. I want the hon. the Postmaster General to get up and apologize for having charged an hon. member with having in his possession improperly and refusing to return the bags belonging to His Majesty or the Post Office Department. I have sat in this House 22 sessions. During the 14 years I sat on that side, and the right hon. gentleman and his colleagues sat on this, and I challenge the right hon. gentleman or any member of his government or any of his supporters, to say that any one of them was ever refused delivery of any parcel or bag addressed to him and sent by express or mail. Neither the Prime Minister nor any of his supporters can say that during the 18 years they sat in opposition they were ever refused any franking privilege, and they sent out tons of literature franked all over the country. But they seem to think that they can ride over us roughshod. They even refuse to allow 'express parcels to be delivered to us. I call upon the Prime Minister to explain by what authority in law any officer of the government has the right to stop an express wagon at the door of parliament and refuse -to allow it to deliver goods to a member of this House. The sergeant-at-arms knows that that has been done this session, and the Postmaster General should explain. That hon. gentleman made ia statement a few moments ago which he knew was not correct. He said that 100 bags came for me on Saturday and 400 on Sunday. Where are they ? Why does he or his officers deny me the right to have these bags here ? Why are they not delivered ? If the bags are there, I want them. The Postmaster General notified an official of the Canadian Express Company not to bring

a bag into the city of Ottawa by express or he would have the company prosecuted.
That is wholly without foundation.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The agent of the express company made that statement since noon. He said that he was notified by the Post Office Department not to carry mail bags by express. He explained that they had not carried a bag since they had received notice that they would be prosecuted if they did. Yet the Postmaster General says that 400 of these bags came in on Sunday. As a matter of fact, 400 parcels came by express, but delivery was refused to me through the interference of officers of the House, under instructions of the Postmaster General.
Perhaps the Postmaster General can explain whether 400 bags did come on Sunday ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The Postmaster General says they came, and we must assume that he would not make a misstatement in this House. Then, the hon. gentleman said that there were not only carloads but train loads of this literature. How many trains would it take to carry 1,800 postal bags ? This gentleman aspiring to be a statesman, occupying the position of Postmaster General, Minister of Labour, a man ' vaster than has been,' rises in this House and makes a statement that one of the little page boys here would know to be absurd. Why, there are hardly enough of these bags to make three or four good wagon loads. Yet, he told us of the trains that would be- required to move these bags from this House. Eighteen hundred bags-and a man could take one on his shoulder, in fact he could carry one under each arm !
The Postmaster General accused us of abusing the franking privilege. Has he any idea of the conditions under which that privilege is to be exercised ? If so, why did he riot call down his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) who went to Toronto, delivered a speech in Massey Hall, then had it printed and hundreds of thousands of copies sent out under his own frank as Minister of Trade and Commerce. Every man in my constituency got a copy of that document, franked by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. That was not only an improper but an illegal thing. Why did not the Postmaster General prevent that action ou the part of his colleague, or why has lie not since called upon him to contribute to the revenue the amount of postage that should have been paid upon these hundreds of thousands of documents sent through the mail. Ministers have the right to send out correspondence, departmental reports and so on ; but they have no right to send out copies of stump speeches, and particularly to have

speechtext: No, I did not.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I do not wonder that he is afraid that it will set the country oil fire
I made no such statement.

speechtext: I suppose he fears that it will arouse such feeling that the militia under my hon. friend from North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) will have to be called out to quiet the people. Well, I have in my hand a copy of this literature, and I intend reading it, so as to put it on ' Hansard,' and I would ask the Postmaster General what part of it is incendiary and seditious ?

The article headed ' To Arms.'
Canada's indictment against the government.
I am sure Canada is practically up in arms against the government for their monstrous scheme. Here we have on this paper a map showing each one of the provinces holding a flag, while the figure representing Canada holds a banner on which is inscribed :
People vs. Government. Broken promises. Wasteful administration. Increasing expenditure. Temporizing with tariff. Legislating for franchise dealers.

Clean politics. Protect Canadian labour agricultural and industrial. Stop wasteful schemes Redeem promises.
The indictment continues:

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: This literature is in two sheets of newspaper form. One of them opens with the heading ' The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Project :	Mr. Borden's Alternative Scheme-Mr. Blair's Sweeping Denunciation of the Cox Project.' Is that an incendiary part of this campaign literature ?
Keep cool.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)

speechtext: Would my hon. friend permit me to interrupt him ? Perhaps the Postmaster General is ready to surrender and apologize for his misdeeds.
Do not deprive ns of the benefit of hearing it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I do not intend to ask him to surrender. As an opposition we are entitled to our rights, and I give the Postmaster General notice that we intend to have them. Then the indictment continues on the next side :
Government by hypocrisy. Platform built to get in upon ; immediately afterwards destroyed Public domains given over to speculators. Attempt to paralyze the sentinel whom Alexander Mackenzie left to guard the treasury. Burdening the Yukon, the Eldorado of Canada with a water concession of bad repute, and a handicap on the mining industry of the nation.
rmWIiat is there incendiary about that ? I. lie Postmaster General must be overflowing with indignation when he charges the leader of the opposition and his supporters with sending out incendiary literature to the people of this country. On the next page I find : $120,000,000 railway.' That is the estimate placed upon it by his own colleague the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals. Surely there is nothing incendiary about that.
To be built for a group of capitalists friendly to the government.
That is why the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals said that Cox could'nt wait,



that there was a ring which could not wait.
Without surveys, without estimates, without information. A reckless scheme that drove the Minister of Railways from the cabinet. Will kill the Intercolonial and sidetrack the canals. 'Cox can't wait.' so the people must pay.
After keeping parliament sitting all summer without disclosing its policy on the transcontinental railway question, the government suddenly announced a scheme at the tail end of the session.
It was an entire surprise to all concerned, and no one knows yet why many of its most absurd features were adopted.
It proposes that the government shall build a railway through an unknown wilderness from Winnipeg to Quebec, and then through the unpeopled forests of New Brunswick to Moncton. The government know so little of the route that they will not attempt even to estimate the cost of the line. Hon. Mr. Blair, whom this scheme drove fo resign the railway portfolio, and who ought to know more about it than any other man, says that it commits the government to an expenditure of $120,000,000. .
Will the Postmaster General get up and explain now what there is incendiary in the remarks I have read thus far ? X propose reading the document through, paragraph by paragraph and line by line, to show what there is incendiary about it. Surely the Postmaster General will withdraw that remark and not force me to read the whole document.

, I have no desire to curtail the right of my hon. friend to read anything lie pleases. Rut if he desires me to allude to that portion of that paper which I regard as incendiary I will do so, at the same time I would not' like to prevent him from reading the intermediate part. The portion to which I alluded is that article headed ' To arms.' Will lie kindly read that article ?
Mr. TAYIjOR. That article is an appeal to the people of this country to take their ballots in their hands and turn the hon. gentlemen out. Is there anything incendiary about that ? The Postmaster General virtually said to-day :	This is an incendiary
document and ought not to he read by the people of this country, therefore I have a right. I, Sir William Mulock, Postmaster General, Minister of Iaibour, the vastest man in this country, the mail who licks the postage stamps for the people of this country, who puts the mucilage on them-I say this is incendiary literature and I won't allow it to go through the post office, and whatever is left after parliament rises we will make a bonfire of it on parliament hill. That is what the minister has said in the argument he made. That is the treatment he is dealing out to the opposition, and Be thinks they are weak and miserable enough to stand it. But he will find out before he gets through that every package of literature that is in these corridors, franked er unfranked, is going to go through the post Mr. TAYLOR.
office, and by his mails, because It is our right.

Will the hon. gentleman permit me another remark?
I have said, and X repeat it again, that this is not a question of the franking privilege.
I have not the slightest desire to interfere, nor could I interfere, with any franking privilege possessed by members of this House.
Now he is surrendering.

No, I am not surrendering. I told the hon. gentleman this morning that this was a matter affecting the department only, that special facilities had to be provided, that the ordinary facilities do not provide for the handling of such a mass of stuff as is now thrown in upon us. I hope the hon. gentleman will not again charge me with seeking to interfere with the franking right of any member.
Mr. TAYIjOR. I absolve the minister from that, because he knows as well as any one what the law is, and he knows he cannot interfere with the franking privilege. But lie knows that as soon as the House is closed that right ceases, and if he can only get along by dribbling out 40 bags a day while the end of the session is in sight and the literature is there, then after prorogation lie will not receive any more of it, because the law says that the franking privilege only lasts while the House is in session, or so, many days after. That is the scheme of the Postmaster General, and I challenge him to get up and deny it.
Certainly, I deny it. The hon. gentleman is romancing. Whatever is posted is m the hands of the post office, and is entitled to go.
Then why did you not take it out of there, and obey the Speaker's order ?
Because there is no place to put it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Let the hon. gentleman sit down. I do not want my speech interfered with.
Whatever is posted has a right to pass through the mails.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
But if the hon. gentleman instructs the Sergeant-at-Arms not to allow any mall matter to come in, how can it pass through the mails ? I paid ?22 express charges upon it, and the Sergeant-at-Arms would not allow it to come inside the House. How could I frank it ? The hon. gentleman has given instructions to the city post office to impound a number of bags addressed to me at the House of Commons, with the re-

suit that mail matter which is sent to the city post office to be delivered to me at the House of Commons is not delivered.

When mail matter arrives at the city post office for delivery at the House of Commons the duty of the post office is completed, and it is prepared to hand over that matter to any officer from the House of Commons who is authorized to receive it. The House of Commons has always taken charge of the delivery of the mails between the House and the city post office. If mail matter is directed to an hon. gentleman it is only waiting his order or the officers of this House authorized to receive it. It is not withheld by the post office. On the contrary, we are most anxious to get rid of it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Then why has not the rule been carried out ? Here is stuff which has been addressed to me at the House of Commons. It has arrived at the city post office. . The gentleman who has the contract for carrying the mail between this House and the city post office brought a load up here, and he was notified by the hon. Postmaster General's officers-
Not at all.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I know what I am speaking about-he was notified to take it back, and he took it back.
By whom ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: By the chief messenger and the Sergeant-at-Arms.
I have nothing to do with that.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Would it have been done if you had not interfered ? Did you, Mr. Speaker, of your own authority, say to the express companies of this city : You cannot [DOT]deliver any mail matter which is addressed to Mr. Taylor at the House of Commons, or any parcel addressed to Mr. Taylor to be delivered to him in his room in the House of Commons ?

I have been asked to make a statement by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) as to the use of the corridors and of the room of the House of Commons. I do it willingly, because I am glad to have the occasion to remove the bad impression under which the hon. member laboured during his remarks_ towards the Speaker of this House, and with regard to some orders which I deemed it my duty to give. A. few days ago my attention was called by some officers of the House to the fact that some of the corridors of the House of Commons were getting filled with mail bags, and without any permission from anybody authorized to give it. We then tried to find a room where those bags could be put, because we 456}
considered that the fact of those bags being in the corridors was not a nice sight for the numerous strangers who happened to visit our parliament buildings. We could not, however, find at first any available room. 1 then gave instructions to ship away those bags as soon as possible, and not to receive any more to be put in the corridors. I was, in doing that, following a precedent of some years ago, when the same question came up. The Speaker at that time ordered that the bags be removed from the sight of the strangers visiting the House. I consider that the corridors of the House of Commons are not available for warehouse or storage purposes. I may be wrong in that respect, but that is the view I entertain upon the question, and until the House decides to the contrary, I think that I am taking a reasonable view of the matter. It has never been my intention to prevent the members of the House who happen to have rooms at their disposal from using them the way they like, and I may say that I have never given any instructions which would deprive any of those members of their entire liberty in that respect. If some statements to the contrary have been made during the discussion, I may say that those statements have been made under an erroneous impression or erroneous information.
Yesterday the hon. member for South Leeds (Mr. Taylor) and a representative of the ' Star ' came to me and asked me whether they could have a room to empty those bags and release them for the use of that paper. We went over the whole ground and found that the only available room was the new Railway Committee room, which I was very glad to put at their disposal. They all seemed to be pretty well satisfied with that arrangement. At all events, the hon. member for South Leeds, who was then present, did not utter a word of dissent. On the contrary, I think he thanked me for what I was doing. I suggested at that interview that perhaps the bags could be put in No. 6, and that it would be more convenient for the members of the opposition. The hon. member for South Leeds went to inquire whether this could be done, and when he returned he said 'no.' Then it was agreed that the Railway Committee room would be at their disposal to empfy those bags and remove the congestion in the corridors. Now, I have been charged with having given orders to prevent the express companies from carrying parcels into room No. 6. I may say that I have never given any instructions of the sort, and the Sergeant-at-Arms reports to me that the orders he has given referred, not to any rooms, but to the corridors, and the parcels addressed to the rooms, so far as he is aware, have not been interfered with. I have every reason to believe that his statement is correct.
A reference has been made also by the hon. leader of the opposition to the fact that

there was a room available down stairs, which was used by some members for mailing' parcels and literature. I think he is misinformed in that respect. Last year, or two years ago, I think that room was occupied by five or six members of this House, and they might have sent parcels or literature from there. Since that room has become a dining room, I am not aware that it has been used for any other purpose. The hon. leader of the opposition also states that he has a small room, but he will be good enough to render me the justice of saying that last year I offered him a larger room, and that he told me he could not very easily take it. X may repeat that I never did prevent any of the members who have rooms from doing what they like with these rooms, but what I did was simply to prevent the corridors being used for storage or warehouse purposes, and in doing that I intended to do only what I considered my duty.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker lias read a statement and has also spoken on behalf of the Sergeant-at-Arms. I say most emphatically that I went to the Sergeant-at-Arms last night and asked him why this stuff was turned away, and he said by instructions. I said : This matter is coming up in the morning, and I am going to take it to my room if I have to carry it myself. He said : You cannot do it. Mr. Speaker did offer to the representatives of the ' Star ' and myself the Railway Committee room, but I immediately asked how we were going to get the bags up there and could we get the messengers. No. we would have to hire our own men to carry it up there.
Why not ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Because the messengers are used by the members of the government and their supporters to carry their literature and to do their messages while we can hardly get one to do an errand for us. The stuff is impounded at the post office and it is impounded at the express office, although it is addressed to myself. That is the position we are placed in. Mr. Speaker makes the statement that the corridors are blocked. They are not being blocked by myself or by any other member of the opposition. These bags have been filled in the post office, carried out and stacked in the corridors for weeks. Why does not Mr. Speaker order the postmaster to remove them ? Yet this is all charged against the opposition whip, who is held responsible for blocking the corridors. It is either the hon. Postmaster General or the postmaster of this House who is at fault in not having this stuff removed, because it has lain there for the past two or three weeks. We have emptied the bags that came in every day, franked them and put them back into the post office. Why should we be charged with causing the blockade ? The Sergeant-at-Arms will not deny that it was by his orders

that our stuff, which came by mail and by express, was turned away. He told me when I brought it up here this morning that I wmuid not be allowed to take it in, but I came prepared to take it in even if I had to carry it in myself. I defy the Sergeant-at-Arms or anybody else to deprive me of my right as a member of this House of taking my express parcels into my room. Here is the position we are in : The Iron. Postmaster General knows very well that if we did not get this stuff franked and Into the post office before the gun fired, or within two or three days after-wards, because I understand there are two or three days of grace, it would not go out to the people of this country. He said it was incendiary, because the electors were called to arms, to vote against this government, and he knows that the people are up in arms against the government. I want to embellish the pages of ' Hansard ' with this, so as to contradict the Postmaster General, who made a statement that he must know was not correct.

Order.
Mr. TAYLOR, I will take that back, Mr. Speaker. If he didn't know it was not correct, he ought to have known it. There is a lot of this stuff piled up on the green outside of the House, and if there comes a shower of rain it may be spoiled.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I want you, Mr. Speaker, to instruct your officers to have that brought in and delivered to me in room No. 6. I want you to order your officers to take in the express matter which they refused to take. I want an order to the chief messenger that the stuff out on the green be brought in. Am I to understand that you do not answer, Mr. Speaker ?

If some stuff was brought for room No. 6 and has not been delivered to room No. 6, it is on account of some misunderstanding between the Sergeant-at-Arm and the hon. member. The Sergeant-at-Arms has just informed me that he has never refused to receive stuff coming to any room.
Mr. TAYLOR, There was a load of this literature came to me by express and the chief messenger refused to receive it.
There must have been a misunderstanding.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The Sergeant-at-Arms told me last night that he could not send down for the express matter which was refused the other night.
As I have said, there must be a misunderstanding, and I trust the hon. gentleman will not pursue that matter further.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Then somebody has backed down. I take the ground that neither

tlie Speaker nor the Postmaster General, nor the Sergeant-at-Arms, nor the chief messenger will deprive me of my lawful rights of having my literature delivered to me. The Postmaster General now says that there are 500 bags addressed to me impounded down in the post office. Will the Postmaster General issue an order to have that sent to me at this House immediately V

There appear to be a great many misunderstandings. I did not say anything about 500 bags being impounded. It is not a fact that any mail matter addressed to the hon. member is impounded at the post office, and not available to him. I have been informed that there are a large number of sacks sent from the ' Star ' office, Montreal, by post to the hon. gentleman, and as we have no storage accommodation for them in the post office proper, they are in the lobby of the post office. We are most anxious that the hon. gentleman should send for them and take them away. What I did state was that one of my officers informed me that there were 400 bags or packages of mail matter sent here on Sunday.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: They were not in the post office ; they were in the express office.
I do not know even that. I was informed that they came to Ottawa, but I do not know whether it is correct or not.
It is none of your business anyway.

It would be if the bags of the post office were used. If my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) would take away one or two hundred bags that are lying there now, lie would accommodate the post office very much, because they are in the way.

I have made inquiry, and I find that 400 parcels, not 400 bags, have come by express, because the right to send them by mail under the franking privilege was denied. I am informed that after they came to Ottawa, an officer of the hon. gentleman's department called upon the express company, and threatened to prosecute because they did not come by mail.
I am sure that is an entire mistake.
That is my information.
Will the hon. gentleman be good enough to give me the name of the officer ?

I do not know the name of the officer, but I will give it to the Postmaster General before the day is over. I am informed that first we were
denied the right of sending them by mail, and then, having sent them at our own cost, by express, the express company, our agent, was threatened with prosecution because he was violating the law in relation to the carriage of mail.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The Postmaster General says that there are at the post office one or two hundred bags of mall matter addressed to me at the House of Commons.
I didn't say that.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: He told me that there were a number o,f bags addressed to me in the lobby of the post office, and he wished I would go down and take them. And he wished I would go and get them.
So I do.
There is free delivery in this city; why do you not deliver them ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Under the franking privilege any parcel sent to me by post should be delivered to me at the post office in the House of Commons; that is the law.
Where is that law ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: And yet the Postmaster General calls on me to go to the city post office, to hire a cart and draw these bags up. Is that the way the hon. gentleman intends to treat the opposition ?

The Post Office Department delivers no mail matter for any member of this House, on this side or on that side. The House itself has always had its own arrangement for conveying this mail matter from the city post office to the House of Commons post office, and1 vice versa, and it is a matter for the committee of this House to deal with.
Who pays for its conveyance between the two post offices ?
The House of Commons.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The jjeople of this country pay for it. The Postmaster General went to the post office and inspected this mail matter and knows that it is addressed to me at the House of Commons, yet it is not sent up here. Who is neglecting his duty ? Why has not that been sent here ? It was sent to the House, but was refused admittance, and was sent back to the post office. Now, Mr. Speaker, what is to become of this stuff which is at the city post office ? I desire an answer.
I have no further statement to make. I do not desire to take any part in the discussion, and I do not think it is becoming for the Speaker to take part in a discussion.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I want information ; is the gentleman who carries the mail from the

city post office to the House of Commons post office under your jurisdiction ? Is the chief messenger of this House under your jurisdiction ? The gentleman who carries the mail from the city post office to this post office brought a load of that to the House ; your chief messenger ordered him to take it back, and would not receive it, and I wish to know who is at fault. I ask the Postmaster General who is at fault, and why I had not possession of the 100 bags which the Postmaster General says he saw at the post office ?

I do not know that my hon. friend will accept my opinion on the subject, but I am quite willing to give it. The whole trouble has arisen from the action of the hon. gentleman in deluging this House with more mail matter than there is accommodation for. The post office accommodation in this building is limited. The building is supplied with a post office room, but that is inadequate to hold the quantity of mail matter that the hon. gentleman desires to have put into it. Whoever approved of the plan of this building in years gone by are to blame, because they did not anticipate this extraordinary condition. However, the bringing of the mails up here is a matter entirely under the control of the House of Commons of Canada. The hon. gentleman is right in saying that the stuff is waiting at the city post office, and I certainly wish with all my heart that the hon. gentleman would make arrangements to remove it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I will have to make an appeal to the Prime Minister. I have been in this House 21 years, 14 years supporting a government when he sat on this side of 'the House, and I would ask him if he ever saw the opposition treated by the Conservative party as the opposition is now being treated by the government ? This matter has been refused admittance to the House ; a load came this morning and is now out on the green. Is that the treatment that the Premier intends meting out to the members of the opposition ?

I do not attach the same importance to this matter as my bon. friend does; perhaps because of the difference in the point of view. I sympathize, however, when he tells us that a lot of this stuff is on the green, and it would be worse if this stuff should be exposed to rain. Perhaps, however, it would extinguish the fire in it if it is incendiary. If my hon. friend bad consulted me earlier, I have not much control over these matters, but I think the resources of the country are adequate to deal with the difficulty, to have the stuff removed from the green, and I think I could undertake to say more, to have ,it carried over and placed on the trains and disposed of.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The Prime Minister is good at making evasive answers. He says the resources of the country are adequate to receive and despatch the mail. If he, as Prime Minister, had an officer at the head of the Post Office Department who would give instructions, it could be done, but the Postmaster General knows that the postmaster in this House has had bags in his possession for three weeks and has not sent them to the city post office; he has authorized the city post office to receive only 40 bags a day, and then he makes the statement that we are to go on at that rate, and that we will be kept here until after Christmas if all of these bags are to be sent out-
So we will.
Will you allow me to have a moment's conference with my hon. friend the Postmaster General, and I think I can soften him ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: While the conference is going on, I shall present to the House-
That is not fair; my hon. friend is like the Boer, when we are in conference he prepares for war. Let me confer with the Postmaster General, and then perhaps we can solve this difficulty.

I would like to say that, so far as using the corridors for warehouse purposes is concerned. I regard you, Mr. Speaker, as having absolute jurisdiction, but not as having jurisdiction to order away from the precincts of the House matters sent by mail or express to any member. From the statement which Mr. Speaker read to the House, we may arrive at the conclusion -that he is of the same opinion and that any occurrence of the kind was due probably to some misunderstanding. As far as using the room down stairs is concerned, I may say that I did not know it was used as a dining room, but as I have not been accustomed to go into the lower precincts so much perhaps as other hon. members, I cannot speak with authority on that point. With respect to my own accommodation, I did not rise for the purpose of making any complaint, although I regard it as somewhat inadequate for the purposes of my work, but I owe apology to you Mr. Speaker, for having forgotten that last year you did offer me somewhat larger quarters, which I did not think I could use, because they were not conveniently situated. I did make an effort to have another room somewhat nearer mine but that did not seem practicable. In what I said this morning, I did not speak, Mr. Speaker, in any personal sense, but on a question of importance as to whether or not any man occupying tbe Chair of Mr. Speaker has the right to

issue the orders which I understood, when I spoke yesterday, had been issued by you, Sir, in this regard. I do not wish to comment on the somewhat sneering terms in which the right hon. the Prime Minister referred to my remarks. He suggested that I desired to put myself on a higher plane than eminent men who have occupied my present position. I trust that my past course in this House is sufficient to justify me from that. If the right hon. gentleman did not enjoy more accommodation in this House than is now given me, the demands of one in my position are perhaps larger than they were years ago-larger because the business of the country is growing and more work has to be done. My right hon. friend speaks of some matters as trifling, for example, whether or not a mass of campaign literature has been addressed and circulated from departments of the government by servants employed and paid by the country. I am not inclined to regard that as so small a matter, and years ago the right hon. gentleman would have been inclined to speak in a different tone regarding it. But that was in the days when he was advocating greater efficiency and purity in the administration of public affairs. I wish to address myself to the practical difficulties of the situation. The Postmaster General says 1,830 bags have been used for this purpose.
At least.

I think that is an outside estimate, if I am correctly informed. But let me point out to the hon. gentleman that 1,830 bags are only a little more than one-half the number which one newspaper in Montreal uses every week. This work began as far back as the 2oth of September. Twenty-six days have elapsed since then. If he had put these bags out at the small number of forty per day, he would have disposed of 1,040.

If the hon. gentleman will allow me I did not say that 1,830 bags was the maximum. 1 said we had given at least 1,830 bags to the ' Star ' people which were used for this purpose. That many we have track of, and my hon. friend will remember that his chief whip said that this stuff began on the 20tli of September.
He did not say ' stuff.'
He said that this stuff began to leave Montreal on the 20th of September and had come at the rate of from fifty to one hundred bags per day-not forty. That would make nearly 3,000.

I have been informed as to the number, of documents sent here from time to time, and according to that information 1,830 bags would cover absolutely everything that has come from Mr. TAYLOR.
Montreal from first to last. I have not counted them but have made some inquiry, and I believe that that is an outside estimate. I know that about 500,000 copies of these documents have been sent out and there are about 300 in each bag. That would be under the estimate which the Postmaster General made this afternoon of 1,830 bags. But if you can distribute 3,000 bags in the course of one week from one newspaper office how is it that from the 25th of September up to the present you have made so little progress in disposing of these bags ?

If my hon. friend will allow me, I will give the reason. The bags that are sent by the ' Star ' newspaper containing its own papers are made up and directed to the post office of each town where the matter is to be delivered. No sorting takes place. Those thousands .of bags are not handled on the cars but go as freight or baggage. They do not go in the postal cars at all.
But they go in Lhe post office.
They do not.
They do when they reach their destination.
That is another matter. We are talking about sending them out.
Are they not in the possession and under the charge of the Post Office Department the moment they are put on the train ?

Certainly, but we are speaking of the work of handling the mail on the cars, and my hon. friend, the leader of the opposition desires to know the exact facts. A newspaper like the * Star ' delivers every day to the railways a large number of bags containing newspapers. Each of these bags is directed to a particular town, and there is no sortation on the cars of the contents. They are not handled in the postal cars at all. They are put into the baggage car so that there is no more difficulty in handling a bag containing 200 or 500 newspapers than in handling a trunk. But each bag of the mail matter to which we are now referring contains many separate pieces. These have to be sorted on the train. The bags of postal matter are put upon the car. When the train starts the clerks have to pour out the contents of the bags upon the table, examine the direction upon each separate piece and put it in the bag for its destination. A considerable space is required in the postal car for the convenience of the officers engaged in that sortation. Therefore, the matter cannot be handled wholesale, as in the case of newspapers going from the office of publication, but must be handled retail, each separate article being subject to separate treatment.
I am obliged tc the Postmaster General for that explana tion. But I understood that, so far as large cities are concerned, the bags have already been so made up.
But still the bags have to be opened In the postal car and their contents examined, because in very few instances do the bags contain only matter for a particular post office.

I think that any difficulty as to that might have been obviated when the bags were filled. If the authorities in the Post Office Department or the post office authorities of the House of Commons had intimated to those engaged in this work that it would be more convenient if the mail matter for a particular place were put in a bag by itself, that would have been done, and that, very likely, would facilitate the work very much. The explanation of the Postmaster General seems to make it abundantly plain that there is no work at all for the Ottawa post office in all this; the work is on the mail car. So far as the Ottawa post office is concerned, it is simply a question of storage, and surely the resources of the government should have enabled them to overcome any difficulty as to storage room. Let me point out this fact to the Postmaster General- that if in Ottawa a paper were to commence publication having a circulation of
15.000	or 20,000, it would give His Majesty's mails more matter to handle than that caused by the distribution of this literature. Yet, I am sure, the Postmaster General would hardly likely stand up in this House and say that the whole mail service in Ottawa would be paralyzed by the mere fact of a newspaper of that magnitude beginning publication here. And let me say also that I am informed-I do not know with what truth, and perhaps we had better have a statement about it if any minister of the Crown is in a position to make known the facts-that the equivalent of twenty-five bags of mall matter has been sent out by m.v lion, friends on the other side as campaign literature every day for the last six or eight weeks. If that has been going on, let us attribute the congestion to that to which it is really due. Let the Postmaster General not send forward the twenty-five or thirty bags of literature on his side, and keep back ours, and then say that the congestion is due to the literature sent out from this side.

On that point, I would like to correct my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax). I have no control over the postmaster of the House of Commons. And, so far as I know, no person has sought in any way to direct or interfere with his actions. You, Mr. Speaker, who have jurisdiction on behalf of the House in these matters. I am sure, , have not interfered Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
w.ith the postmaster in the proper discharge of his duties. The postmaster has discharged his duties as he thought best and if he is showing partiality, as an officer of the House lie is amenable to the discipline of the House. But I am sure there is no foundation for the suggestion that literature from one side has received preference or priority over the other. There has been the utmost fairness, and no partiality has been shown.

I was not accusing any officer of partiality or unfairness. But I am credibly informed by those who profess to know what they speak about that mail matter equivalent to twenty-five bags a day has been sent out by my hon. friends opposite for the last six or eight weeks.
And by my hon. friends on that side.
The result of that is a certain congestion.
Caused by both sides.

That is exactly what I am coming to. But, up to the present time, we have been (old that it has been caused by the literature sent out by this side. And we have heard of the scandalous abuse of the franking privilege, and so on. Let us understand that both sides arc. engaged in the work of propagating their political views by sending out their campaign literature during the session of parliament under franks. But, when that occasions congestion, let us not have ministers standing up in the House and accusing members on this side of causing that congestion, and let us not have a stoppage, and the piling up of that literature in these corridors, the stoppage applying only to the literature from this side. That is all we ask. We simply desire that our rights in that regard shall be the same as those of others, that there shall not be all this comment and excitement because we are doing what is quite within our right to do, and what hon. gentlemen on the other side are doing in exactly the same way, and, as I believe on a very much larger scale.
Oh, no. The hon. gentleman does not believe that.

Well, I will take my hon. friend's word that it is not greater. There is another remark as to how this mail matter accumulates. It came in by mail up to the time we were driven to send it by express, which we did until the express company were threatened, as I am informed, with prosecution for carrying matter that should be sent by mail-it lias come here in some way without great apparent difficulty ; but it is only when we try to send it away from here that the congestion is caused. The

explanation of my hon. friend as to the necessity of sorting on t lie train accounts for it in part. But, even with that explanation,' I do not see that there should be the congestion which is said to have resulted merely through our effort to send out what seems to me a very moderate amount of campaign literature. I do not think it is desirable to have this condition of affairs continue. It seems to me that means could be found to prevent this congestion. I am sure that my hon. friend the Postmaster General and the Prime Minister, if they should have this conference spoken of a little while ago, will devise some means by which a result will be arrived at satisfactory to all the members of the House. And I shall be glad if when my right hon. friend (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has arrived at a conclusion with regard to it, he will give a statement as to what we may expect on this question which has already occupied a considerable length of time.

The unfortunate thing about this debate is, that the employees of this House will be encouraged to treat members of parliament with disrespect. I think members of parliament, on both sides, should stand together, to preserve the respect due to this House. By so doing we maintain the honour of the people of Canada. I am persuaded, that the conduct of the Postmaster General will give the employees of the House the impression, that they can treat members of the opposition with less respect than they show to members supporting the government. It would be unworthy and dishonourable for members of this House to occupy that position, not because they are members of the government side of the opposition, but because they represent the constituencies of this country. So far as service is due by members of parliament, I do not make the slightest distinction between those who support the government and those who support the opposition.
Now, I want to say first that I think the Prime Minister should apologize to our leader. I am not inclined to make unkind remarks. In taking part in the debates of this House I have always endeavoured to exercise courtesy. If a man is not strong enough to say what he wants to say in measured language, then he is not a very strong man. Now, I think the Prime Mini-ister should apologize to the leader of the opposition for saying, as he did this morning, that the language used by the leader of the opposition was unworthy of himself. 1 think the language of the leader of the opposition was mild and measured in the extreme. If we have any complaint to make on this side against the leader of the opposition it is that he always fights with gloves when he fights the hon. gentlemen opposite, that he is too courteous to the gentlemen who sit opposite. After that has
been the leading feature of his conduct towards the government, it strikes me that the Prime Minister was not well advised when he made that remark. I think the language is peculiarly unworthy of the Prime Minister himself. It is cutting language, and I would not have blamed the leader of the opposition if he had resented it with much more lire and spirit than he did. But with his usual courtesy he permitted the Prime Minister to go almost scott free. I do not propose to do that, and I wish the Prime Minister to apologize to the leader of the opposition for departing from the traditional good manners that should characterize a Prime Minister of Canada.
Now, the Prime Minister said that he had occupied that room when in opposition and he never complained. He ought to have complained. If he, the leader of the opposition, was shut up in that little room, he ought to have had more respect for his position and he should have complained. I am going to complain, and I will never stop complaining until every member of this House is treated with proper respect. When I am at home-and I think it is the same with reference to every other gentleman-I have a house, I have an office, where, if a gentleman wishes to consult me privately, he can do so. I have typewriters, an office fitted up with the usual appliances to enable me to attend to the business of my clients. When I come here I come representing 25,000 people of the county of Colchester, whose business I have to attend to, and how am I treated here ? I have no room, I have not the slightest opportunity to do the business that is imposed upon me. But I do not wish to be a loafer, I wish to work and perform the duties that are cast upon me. But when I come here, I am encouraged to be a loafer and an idler. I am put into a large room which is more like a club-room, where there are eight, or ten, or twenty gentlemen smoking and talking together. How can I do the business of
25,000	people in such quarters as that V Yet that is the accommodation that is furnished to me, and I am going to tell the people of Colchester that this government and this parliament are to blame for it. that this government treats myself and treats them with the utmost disrespect in neglecting to furnish me with a private apartment in which I can do the business of my county. Up in this part of country it appears that only the ministers are supposed to have any business to do. I am charged with responsibilities as well as they are, and I want some place assigned to me in which I can do the business of my constituents. As it is, T had to go into the library and crave from the librarian the courtesy of an alcove in which to do the business of a member of parliament. But it is far from being a place to do business in, because you are interrupted. A gentle-

1458a
man who is accustomed to work wants privacy. But we are deprived of all that and it is only the ministers who have apartments.
When we appoint a judge of the Supreme Court/ of Canada we assign him two or three rooms in which to do his business. It is not nearly as important that he should have two or three rooms as it is for a member of parliament. A judge of the Supreme Court does not deal with the interests of more than 200 or 300 suitors in a year. I have charged upon me the interests of 25,000 suitors in this parliament. Why should we give a judge a couple of rooms in which to do his business, and not assign one room to a member of parliament, who has vastly more important duties ? I charge upon the members of this parliament, who have represented this country for the last thirty years, in having been derelict to their duty in allowing themselves to be treated with absolute disrespect. The members of this House should supply themselves first of all with accommodation. If we appoint a clerk he is at once given a room of his own. See what contumely is heaped upon the members of this House in treating them with less respect than a clerk. We appoint a man to a position and give him a salary of $1,200 or $1,500 a year. Do we ask him to sit out on the green to do his business ? Do we ask him to sit on one of these bags ? No, we do not, we assign him a room. Why, the very instant we employ the meanest clerk in the House of Commons we assign him a room. They have intelligence enough, but it is impossible for any one to do work without a room, therefore, we assign the meanest employee a room of his own. I blame the members of parliament for permitting this indignity to be heaped upon them-the members of parliament on both sides of the House, and not only of this parliament, but of all preceding parliaments.
I desire to say further that I think the Postmaster General has been led into this difficulty through listening to over zealous partisans. For my part I would be a long time in this House, I would be ten years in this House, going up and down these corridors, before I would make a complaint to anybody about these bags. They are piled up there, and if some gentleman in going home late at night feeling tired and sick, passing between those tiers of bags on each side of him, it would be an assistance to him, in case any accident happened, to find a soft bed on which to fall. There should not be very much complaint. Why should any gentleman going through those corridors object to these bags being there unless he were a partisan ? I undertake to say that the hon. Postmaster General allowed himself to be used by some ungracious partisan on his side who went to him and represented to him that he should interfere with the opposition in the pursuit Mr. GOURLEY.
of their duty. He pulled his leg, as it were, and instead of telling this partisan that he did not want to interfere with the opposition, the hon. Postmaster General listened to him and became a partisan himself. X do not believe that hon. gentlemen opposite sympathize with the hon. Postmaster General. I believe there is too much courtesy and refinement amongst hon. gentlemen od-posite to sympathize with anything like this mean partisanship which has been shown in connection with this matter. I regret this partisanship very much. There are partisans on both sides but the leading men of the party on both sides ought to be strong enough to teach them better manners. The hon. Postmaster General says that a complaint was made by a newspaper in Montreal. Then he is the victim of the mere jealousy of some newspaper in Montreal. Some newspaper is perhaps jealous of the ' Star ' and wants to give the ' Star ' some trouble in respect to its mail matter. The hon. Postmaster General should have told the newspapers to settle their jealousies between themselves, that the urgent need of more mail bags will pass away in two or three days, and he should not have permitted himself to have been drawn into the matter in the way in which he has been. That hon. gentleman represents the dignity of this House in some measure and in some measure the dignity of the country and he should not have permitted himself to have been dragged into a mere petty quarrel between some newspapers in Montreal. He should have been the first man to have stood up and fought for the dignity of this House. He should have said that the members of this House had privileges. I charge the hon. Postmaster General with not standing up for the dignity of this House. It is the duty of every member of this House to preserve the dignity of those on both sides, A minister ought not to be a partisan when it comes to preserving the respect of the people for this House. I will always stand up for the respect which is due to this House. We should have respect for ourselves. We should conduct our debates with courtesy and decency and we should stand together in the preservation of our rights in order that the country may respect us and respect parliament. I think the hon. Postmaster General forgot himself when this newspaper came to him and made the complaint to which he refers. When this newspaper complained to him that they had not sufficient bags, the hon. Postmaster General should have inquired into the matter and if he found out that members of parliament in the exercise of their franking privilege had used up the supply of bags he should have said to that newspaper:	Wait, your business is
private. You have a little private newspaper to run. The bags are being used by members of parliament for the dissemination of public information all over the

country, which is more important than the dissemination of any private newspaper. If he had had any self respect he would have said on behalf of this House that the privileges of a member of parliament are superior to the privileges of a newspaper. The hon. Postmaster General said that a manufacturer in some small country town could not get his manufacturing circulars sent through the post office for three days because the post office was occupied by literature sent out by members of parliament. I undertake to say that such a statement is an insult to this parliament. He should have told that manufacturer that it was our duty to send out literature to the country rather than that the post office should be occupied with the literature that he desired to send out. I take the ground that it is our duty to send out literature. The people in my constituency are complaining because there is no literature sent out. They say that the members of parliament are lazy and that we are not performing our duty if we do not send out literature while we are here. The people pay the bills, they have a right to have literature sent to them and it is the first duty of the Post Office Department to send out'literature from this House for the purpose of educating the people. If the government have a wise policy they should be the first to want literature sent out, because, if their policy is wise, the literature we send out will only exhibit that policy in a better light. Therefore, if I were supporting a government which I believed to be a strong government I would urge the opposition to send out literature, because, if the policy of the government were a desirable one, the opposition would make out a weak case. The people are just as competent to criticise an argument as we are and in many cases there are many more intelligent men outside of this House than there are inside of it. While there is a fair proportion of intelligence inside of this House there are many men outside of this House who are far in advance in the matter of intelligence than men inside of this House. Hon. gentlemen opposite should not interfere with political organization but they should rather encourage us.
Order.

One or two hon. gentlemen of ill manners can make a noise. They should encourage us in our organization. They should give us every facility for organization because this country is governed by parties and it is in the highest interests of the country that every bit of knowledge that can assist the electors in arriving at the verdict as to which party shall rule the country should be presented to their minds. Every bit of information should be scattered broadcast. That is the basis of the franking privilege. The franking privilege is the privilege of the people. It is not my privilege, it is not the privilege of any other hon. member, but it is the privilege of the people to get literature from this parliament free, because, if you charged the cost of sending out literature to an individual member, it would he impossible for him to send it out. Therefore, the people have wisely decreed that members of parliament shall have the liberty of sending out literature through the country free. Recollect you put into our hands the most powerful weapon when we can go to the country and say : You dare not allow us to exercise the privilege of sending out literature, because your crimes and misconduct are such that you do not want them to be known. Consequently I for one would say that the lion. Postmaster General should get up, recall every order that lie has given and if necessary order
5,000	bags to-night. What is the cost of a few bags compared with this attack upon the privileges of parliament ? And if necessary he should have a few extra postal cars. If the hon. Postmaster General were a business man rather than have this matter exploited he would have ordered 5,000 additional bags and hired some postal cars and had this literature removed from day to day. Surely the Post Office Department of Canada is strong enough to remove this literature. What a confession that after six yeArs of administration by the hon. Postmaster General the post office service has become so inefficient, so impotent, so weak, that it is impossible to move a few hags of mail from the corridors of this House.
I did not think that the Post Office Department had been so emaciated by the administration of the hon. Postmaster General as to leave it in this unhappy state. I think the hon. Postmaster General should give instructions at once, no matter what it costs, to have these corridors cleared and to have the stuff transmitted through the mails. I think also that the right hon. leader of the government should apologize to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition and that the hon. Postmaster General should apologize to the House for this serious attack upon the privileges of every member of parliament.

With the desire that we should endeavour to proceed with the business of the House, I have had a conference with my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock), and he Informs me that he has ordered 1,000 bags. They cannot be made in *i day, but they will be made on short notice. If my hon. friend (Mr. Borden) will allow me to proceed with the businesss of the House, I can confer with him, and I think we can come to a satisfactory arrangement.

That will be satisfactory.
Motion (Mr. Borden, Halifax) to adjourn the House negatived.

maintopic: SUPPLY-QUESTION OP PRIVILEGE BY MR. WALTER SCOTT.

speechtext: Tlie MINISTER OP FINANCE moved that the House again go into Committee of Supply.

maintopic: SUPPLY-QUESTION OP PRIVILEGE BY MR. WALTER SCOTT.
speechtext:
Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. In one of these sheets of that campaign literature, which has been the subject of debate all day, I find that I am charged with the serious offence of lowering the tone of debate in this House. There is an article headed :
' Lowering the tone of debate; Liberal backbenchers resort to abusive tactics and barroom politics.' This sheet is gotten up in a form that might lead some people to believe that it was a veritable official document; it has the national coat of arms at its head, and it would almost remind one of the celebrated proclamation once isssued to the Indians instructing 'them how to cast their ballots.

maintopic: SUPPLY-QUESTION OP PRIVILEGE BY MR. WALTER SCOTT.
speechtext: Or the bogus ' Globe.'

maintopic: SUPPLY-QUESTION OP PRIVILEGE BY MR. WALTER SCOTT.
speechtext: Or the bogus ' Globe,' as my bon. friend says. I and some other members of the House are charged with lowering the tone of debate and degrading this parliament-I presume that the' exhibition we have seen to-day from gentlemen opposite is calculated to restore the tone of debate. Those of us who are charged with this offence have, according to this sheet, precipitated a crisis in this country, and the people are called to arms on account of that crisis in national politics. And why is this ? It is because one lion, gentleman on this side called an official of a railway company 'a red-headed boy'; because another hon. gentleman applied the term ' a raw young person ' to some one outside of the House ; because it was said that one hon. gentleman ' displayed his ignorance ' ; and because the words ' intellectual paralysis ' were used in another case. The fact that these epithets were applied has, according to this sheet, brought on a crisis in our national affairs, and in consequence the saving remnant of the people are called to arms. My own offence is that I made reference to certain railway companies, namely, the Qu'-Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan and the Calgary and Edmonton Companies, in connection with which I made an allusion to my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier). I wish to explain my position, in face of this charge which must be considered somewhat serious. I wish to state that when I referred to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) I did not mean to reflect in the slightest degree upon his honesty or personal honour. I have some right to complain that a disposition has been shown on the part of some members of this House, and on the part of a section of the press,, as well as in this campaign document, to read into the

maintopic: SUPPLY-QUESTION OP PRIVILEGE BY MR. WALTER SCOTT.
speechtext:
words I used a meaning w'liich these words were not intended to convey, and which I do not believe they do convey. On the contrary, I would like to have permission to state, with regard to my bon. friend (Mr. Osier), that I believe he holds his public position in this country at a very considerable personal and financial sacrifice, as do many other members of this House. It is an encouraging thing that men of bis calibre, men of very extensive business interests, are found willing to sacrifice their personal and financial convenience to hold public positions. I repeat that I did not make, and that I do not intend to make any reflection on the honour or honesty of my hon. friend from West Toronto. My reference to him was made in perfect good faith. Beyond having verified from the reports of the Department of Railways and Canals the figures on which my reference was based I had not, however, immediately before making the reference, looked very closely into these particular matters. I thought they were matters of common knowledge, and 'while the direct and absolute way in w'hieh my statement was challenged by my hon. friend (Mr. Osier) left me no recourse but to retract, it did surprise me exceedingly. Later I took occasion to examine into such of the facts as were available to me. The House lias had some notice of this by the series of questions which some days ago I put upon the Order paper. I had, nevertheless, concluded to make no further reference to the matter until the serious charge against me in this campaign sheet was called to my attention. I think the House will agree with me that the very widespread accusation which is made in this sheet-stating that my personal conduct has been such as to degrade parliament-renders it incumbent on me to set myself right. I trust that the facts which I will endeavour very briefly to place before the House will lead my hon. friend from West Toronto to set me in the right with regard to his accusation that 1 had knowingly and wilfully made a false accusation against him. On looking further into the case, I found these facts: First, notwithstanding that by law railway bondholders' mortgages are required to'be deposited in the office of the Secretary of State, no such document with respect to the Qu'-Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan is in that office. I have, therefore, been unable to verify the assertions of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) with respect to that particular railroad. I find, however, that in the statutes of 3890 (chap. 82), confirming the agreement made between the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskacbewan Company and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, subclause (E) of section 1 of this agreement, sets out :
The company shall not issue any bonds, secured directly or indirectly on its land subsidies or any portion of such land subsidies.
*

My hon. friend (Mr. Osier) declared, if I understood him aright, that the $3,809,140 bond issue of that company, was only floated by the additional pledge of the total land subsidy. That statement of his, and the clause of the agreement, do not appear to harmonize, and some further explanation from the hon. gentleman would be in order. I may point out that there is another rather suspicious looking clause in the agreement, which is to be found in chapter 82 of the statutes of 1890. 'Subclause (C) of section 3 of the agreement sets out as follows :
It is understood and declared that the Qu'Ap-pel'le Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway Company may transfer one half of its land subsidy to any person or persons as it may deem proper.
However, as I said, the mortgage is not deposited in the office of the Secretary of State, and I was able to find no particular facts with regard to that road or that company. But by chapter S4 of the statutes of 1890, in an Act to incorporate the Calgary and Edmonton Railway Company, I find that the name of my hon. friend the junior member for West Toronto- (Mr. Osier) appears amongst the names of those incorporated as the company to whom we voted 6,400 acres of land per mile for 340 miles of road, and to whom we granted $1,600,000 in cash, in twenty equal annual payments. Now, I find also, in the mortgage deed of the Calgary and Edmonton bondholders, this provision :
It is, however, expressly understood that the land grant fro-m the government shall be excepted from the operation of the said mortgage and shall form no part of the security for the payment of the said bonds or the interest thereon.
Now, I appeal to my hon. friend if the discrepancies between these matters of record and what I understood him to state on a former occasion in this House are not sufficient to at least call for some further explanation from him. He stated, if I understood him accurately, that he was not one of those who obtained tin? new Calgary and Edmonton charter in 1890, but, on the contrary, I find that his name appears in the Act. I also understood him to state that in order to raise the amount of money- the exact sum was $5,474,513-which was the proceeds of the Calgary and Edmonton bonds, the land grant had to be pledged to form part of the security, or. as he put it. the land grant was sold with the bonds for the above sum. Now, the clause in the mortgage which I have read would seem to indicate that the contrary was the fact.
Let me give my hon. friend a very brief analysis of the figures of this contract. The proceeds of the bonds sale in connection with the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and. Saskatchewan Railway were $3,809,140, while the cost of the road was $2,539,600. There is a balance there of $1,269,540, which my hon. friend explained was left in the hands
of bankers to guarantee six years' interest. By my calculation six years' interest at 6 per cent upon the amount of the bonds would be $1,371,288. The surplus as between the proceeds of the bonds and the actual cost of the road was $1,209,540, so that upon the money raised by- the bonds there would appear to be a shortage in this matter of interest for six years of $101,748.
