Does my hon. friend contend that it took a land grant of 1,619,200 acres to cover this deficiency of, roundly, $100,000, which appears to be the shortage in the six years' interest ?
The results with regard to the Calgary and Edmonton are very similar. The proceeds of the bonds were $5,474,513, while the actual cost of the road appears by the records in the Railway and Canals Department to have been S3.743.562. There is a surplus there of $1,730,951, which, as my hon. friend said; was left in the hands of bankers. At 6 per cent, six years' interest upon the total bond issue would amount to $1,970,820. and to cover that amount there was a surplus between the bond issue and the actual cost of the road of $1,730,951, so there would be a shortage there from the amount necessary to cover the interest of about $240,000 in round numbers. I ask. with regard to this, does my hon. friend contend that a land grant of 1.8S8.000 had all to be pledged to cover this $240,000 : and if so. what became of the paid-up capital stock, which on the Calgary and Edmonton road, is put at an amount of $1,000,000? I shall send these figures and calculations over to my hon. friend, and he will be able to see whether or not they are accurate.
It certainly appears to me to be almost impossible that it should have been found necessary to pledge the whole land grant to provide for these comparatively small amounts of money. If the land grant were not pledged, as appears to be indicated by the clause of the mortgage which 1 have read, then the question is, what became of the land grant ? On looking into this phase of the matter, I have found that of the land grant earned by the Calgary and Edmonton Company ail area of 1,139,700 acres has already been patented, and to whom ? The railway company, of which my hon. friend, I believe, is a member, has secured patents on 215,816 acres. Nominees of the railway company have secured 57,576 acres. The firm of Osier, Hammond & Nanton have secured patents for 25,140 acres. Mr. James Ross has received patents for 41,130 acres. Assignees of Mr. Ross have received 105 acres. The Calgary and Edmonton Land Company has received the greatest amount, it has received patents for 792,799 acres, and 'assignees of the land company have been given patents for 12,510 acres. Now, as I pointed out, the land company has obtained the big slice, nearly SOO.OOO acres, which, in my opinion, is worth $2,500,000 to-day if it is worth a cent. I found fur-

tlier that my hon. friend is a member and a director of this Calgary and Edmonton Land Company, which is a different concern from the railway company. He appears to be a member of both the railway and the land company, both of which have participated, as I have shown, in the land grant.
Let me go over this ground again briefly. The Calgary and Edmonton Railway actually cost $3,743,572, which, I may remark, my hon. friend assured the House on a former occasion, was every bit paid in cash. The bond issue was $18,500.per mile for 300 miles ; this appears in the mortgage deed. But the actual proceeds of the bonds seem to have been only $5,474,513, being roundly $75,000 less than their apparent par value. Between the proceeds and the cost of the road there Is a difference of $1,730,951. This sum my hon. friend said-and I believe him implicitly-was left with the banks as a guarantee of the payment of interest-and I have shown that the annual interest at 6 per cent would amount to only $328,470-so that this surplus would evidently, with the exception of a shortage of only about $240,000, meet the total interest of 6 per cent for the whole period of six years.
Let me remark further that considering the fact that these bonds were put on the market with the virtual assurance to the purchasing public on the other side that the Canadian Pacific Railway would, in a certain number of years, take them up at the price of 110, and considering further that the full interest for six years was guaranteed, less only a matter of $240,000, these bonds must have been satisfactory to the purchasing public. Surely that guarantee ought to have been considered ample. In the last annual report of the Canadian Pacific Railway, I find the fact recorded that the total bond issue of the Calgary and Edmonton Company has been taken up by the Canadian Pacific Railway at par, and that the Canadian Pacific Railway has further paid $500,000 for the paid up capital stock of $1,000,000, which my hon. friend, on a former occasion, told the House was not all paid in cash originally; and at all events, both the bondholders and the railway company seem to have come out of the deal very successfully, wholly apart from the land grant. I have no wish to go further Into the merits of this matter or to press it any further, but I would ask my hon. friend to do me the justice of admitting that these facts-which I believe are facts and which I only had in a general way in my mind when making my first allusion-go to show that I did not knowingly and wilfully make any false accusation against him.

maintopic: SUPPLY-QUESTION OP PRIVILEGE BY MR. WALTER SCOTT.
speechtext:
I did not intend to make any reply to this renewed attack upon me, coming at this time of the session. I can hardly understand it. I have explained very fully my connection with this road. I have pointed out where Mr. SCOTT.
the figures that have been quoted are wrong. I explained that the land was sold with the bonds to a syndicate, which is a very common way of doing these transactions, and that the whole money realized was expended on the construction of the road and in paying the interest. The only point I would make now in reply is regarding my previous statement, which might be misconstrued, from tiie fact that my name is on the directorate of the present Calgary Railway Company. I made the statement that I was not directly or indirectly connected with the inception of either the Saskatchewan and Long Lake or the Calgary and Edmonton Road. I was not a promoter, in any shape or form, of either of those roads. I came in after the original promoters had failed, and at the request of the late Sir John Macdonald. When I spoke on a previous occasion, I did not know thoroughly the history of the older incorporations ; but Mr. Nicol Kingsinill, K.C., whose name is well known to this House, and who had been connected with those two roads long before I had anything to do with them, has given me the following memo concerning their origin and inception :-
October 19th, 1903.
E. B. Osier, Esq.. M.P.,
Toronto Club,
Toronto, Ont.
My Dear Osier.

Re Qu'Appelle, Long Lake & Saskatchewan Railway Company.
This company was formed by an amalgamation with the South Saskatchewan Valley Railway Company, a list of the directors of which I now inclose also ; a list of the incorporators of the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railroad and Steamboat Company.
I was employed by the late Senator Mac-Innes and Mr. Andrew Onderdonlc to endeavour to get the assistance of the government to this railway, after the first 25 miles had been built.
The affairs of the company were in a very low condition financially, and Mr. Onderdonk had been called in by the late Senator Mac-Innes to endeavour to undertake the construction of the railway. Mr. Onderdonk made an offer to the government, but no arrangement was made, and it was. if I mistake not, some time subsequent to this that you lent your assistance and carried the railway to completion. I was acting for the contractors who constructed the road, but in this you had no interest.
Re Calgary and Edmonton Railway Company :
As regards this company, as you are aware,. I was one of the incorporators, and have been upon its board ever since until two or three months ago, when it was passed over to the Canadian Pacific Railway ; and I am also aware of all the circumstances which preceded its construction.
The Calgary and Edmonton was preceded by a line called ' The Alberta and Athabasca Railway Company,' incorporated July 20, 1885. The name of this company was changed afterwards to 'The Northwestern Railway Company of Canada,' in 1889. The original incorporators are on the memorandum I inclose, and the directors added by the Act of 1899, you will also find on such memorandum. This company was brought before capitalists in

England, and Praed's Bank were interested in it ; one of the Lloyds was sent out to make an examination, and reported so favourably that it was supposed they would be able to finance the transaction ; they had a large land subsidy, but no cash subsidy ; the land subsidy was 10,000 acres a mile. After attempting to finance the matter, they finally failed;
I know this personally, as I went and saw the Praed people in London, and received a letter from them stating that they had been unable to do anything and must withdraw.
After this occurred the government, who were exceedingly anxious that the line to Edmonton should be constructed, as a preventive to further troubles with the Indians, asked Mr. Ross to take up the project, and the Act incorporating this railway company was applied for and obtained at the instigation and request of the government of the Dominion; this I am personally aware of, as I had the conduct of the negotiations with the government at the time, and the making of the contract. It was, if I mistake not, at this juncture, that you first had anything to do with the-transaction ; and you and Mr. Ross went to England and raised the necessary money. The government were so anxious that this railway should be constructed that they passed the original Order in Council for the subsidy, subject to the sanction of parliament, before such sanction was obtained, and it was upon this order that the financial arrangements in England were commenced.
These facts are shown in the draft petition of right which we were about filing against the government, for the purpose of obtaining a settlement of the land grant, a settlement which was afterwards made. I inclose you a draft of the suggested petition of right, the value to you of which will be that you can absolutely depend upon any statement that is made in this draft being correct, it having been made up for the purpose of having the opinion of counsel. There is a good deal of it which is merely historical, and has relation to the land dispute with the government. Be good enough to send me back this printed draft petition of right in the Exchequer Court, as it is the only copy I have.
Trusting that this will supply the information you needed, believe me,
Yours very faithfully,
(Sgd.) VICAL KINGSMILL.
South Saskatchewan Valley Railway Company, Incorporated by 43 Victoria, Chapter 66, assented to May 7, 1880.
Names of persons incorporated :-Andrew Robertson, Donald Maclnnis, John Ross, M. H. Cochrane, Duncan McIntyre, J. R. Thibaudeau, James Turner.
Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskathewan Railroad and Steamboat Company, incorporated by 46 Victoria, Chapter 72, assented to May 25,1883.
Names of persons incorporated :-Robert Doull. William B. Searth, Oliver T. Stone, John A. Mackenzie, J. J. Foy, Edgar Dewdney, Gilbert R. Pugsley.
Alberta and Athabasca Railway Company, incorporated by 48 and 49 Victoria, Chapter 8S, assented to July 20, 1885.
Names of persons incorporated :-Henry B. Beard, George F. Jackson, William W. Huntingdon, John S. McEwen, Louis Sands, Arthur T. H. Williams, R. P. Russell. A. B. Nettle-ton, Samuel P. Snider, C. C. Colby.
Directors added by the Act, assented to April 16, 1889, 52 Victoria, Chapter 65 :-
Mackworth Bulkley Praed, John Maurice Lloyd, John Dale and James Lloyd, all of London, Eng.; Charles T. Drummond, William White, and C. C. Colby.
I do not wish to take up the time of the House at present. The facts are as I have stated. My previous statements to my connection with these companies, and as to the disposition of the land and of the money received, is absolutely correct; and so far from being a company promoter, so far from my having had anything to do with the original conception of that road, that road was forced upon the attention of Mr. Ross and myself afterwards by the late Sir John Macdonald. I shall not weary the House with going into this long petition of rights, but I may say that it contains letters from Sir John Macdonald to Mr. Ross urging him to take the road up and to go forward at once on the Order in Council, andpro-misingthat a subsidy would be voted by parliament, and declaring that he would be perfectly justified in submitting his proposition to the capitalists in London. That was done, and the securities were disposed of as X have said, and the money realized from the securities provided for the construction of the railway and for the payment of the interest on the bonds and other debts. Two years ago, when this matter was brought up, I explained very fully my connection with the company. I have only to repeat that every statement I made with respect to that road isl absolutely correct.

Before leaving the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring a matter before the House which should have received the attention of the government before this time, the question of some additional pension to those who served in South Africa and suffered more or less disability. I am sorry to think that men in that position in this country have remained three years without receiving any consideration at the hands of the government. I do not at all advocate that the people of any country should be induced, by what may be offered' in the sense of recognition of service, to enlist in the ranks of the army ; but I think that the people's gratitude should be expressed towards those who have risked life and limb in defence of the common rights. I have in my own constituency a case which certainly is deserving of more recognition than it has so far been given by the government. I refer to Trooper Mulloy, blind Trooper Mulloy, a boy born and brought up in the county I have the honour to represent. I have known his family for years. They are in every sense respectable, deserving people; and this young man, who is a man of more than ordinary ability, ambitious, active and fairly well educated, went into the South African war and suffered total disability by loosing

tile sight of both eyes. He receives, from the British government a pension of G5 cents per day. That is altogether inadequate for the maintenance of an individual in this country. He is now pursuing his course at college, endeavouring to get an education, that he may be able so far as possible, to take care of himself in the world. I am sure I do not appeal to this House in the way of charity on behalf of this young man and others like him ; but I appeal to the sense of justice of those who took the post of danger at the time of the country's trial. When he returned to Liver pool he made what I may call that Spartan speech, that for him the past had no regrets. And that speech has gone around the world wherever the English language is spoken, and it is echoing and re-echoin through this country to-day. That youug man is struggling without sight, endeavour ing to get an education that he may put himself, even though he has lost his sight, upon an equal footing with other men. And the government have given no attention to these cases-nothing has been done. I bring this forward not to criticise the government, but to try to impress upon them the idea that this is a thing that should be attended to, and that the services of these young men should be recognized. We may talk as we please about this country abroad and in the eyes of the world, but the going of these young men from Canada did more to bring this country into prominence than any other thing that has been done in the last twenty-five years. I refer to Trooper Mu,lloy, not because I would single him out from among others who are also deserving, but because I am acquainted with all the circumstances of his case, and his ease teaches me how deserving all these others are. I am quite aware that these men are not in the same position as the young men, for instance, who went out at the time of the rebellion of 1885, and who received pensions, some of them receiving special treatment at the hands of the government. But, though they are not in the same position towards the Canadian government. I say they are just as deserving. The S >uth African question was a colonial question. It was a question involving the rights of the colonists which were invaded by those who had no right to invade them ; and those who went out to fight for Britain's cause in South Africa were fighting to maintain colonial interests as much as were the men who put down the rebellion in the North-west. I have here a return, brought down for the information of the House of Commons, showing those who received pensions because of disability resulting from services in 1885. I find that some received special treatment; for instance, Captain Peters received $1,0(10 a year. That was away above and beyond the ordinary rule.
And he only lost an arm.

And, as the hon. member says, he only lost an arm, while Trooper Mulloy suffered total disability, and so deserves special treatment at the hands of the government. I am sure the country will bear out the Prime Minister in recognizing the claims of the men who served in South Africa, and I hope he will give this matter his attention at an early day. Three years, I am sure, is quite long enough for these young men to wait, querying whether or not they are to receive recognition from their country. An example has been set up by the people to the south of us. I do not say that we should follow that example. The American people are paying $138,000,000 a year now to men who were in the war of 1861-65. They Say to the men who took part in that war :	Even though
you may have only served in the ranks, your country remembers your service ; and if you are injured or suffer disability even in the ordinary avocations of life, you shall receive a pension. I do not say that I would advocate a similar course in this country, But their example teaches us a lesson. That country is permeated with patriotism so far ns American rights are concerned-and we have just had a lesson of that-and their soldiers know that the sympathy and help of their country can be depended upon. I want to say on behalf of these South African boys, that the people of this country, irrespective of party or race, I believe, are ready to support anything reasonable that the government may choose to do in recognition of their bravery.

I wish to support strongly every word that has been uttered by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Broder). Although he has spoken particularly of one case, he has included all cases. I am ready to support a special recognition of the particular ease he mentioned, and I hope there will be a general willingness to support a recognition of all cases of disability suffered by our soldiers in South Africa. I do not know that I can say anything more than he has said, and I do not think I can say it as well as he has said it. But I wish to emphasize everything he has said, and the way he has said it. I can perhaps speak the more feelingly on this matter, because as I have already taken occasion to inform the House, the constituency which I represent sent more men to South Africa than any other in the Dominion of Canada. There are men throughout that constituency who have suffered serious disability because of their patriotism, patriotism of the highest type. I do not wish to imply that the men who served in the North-west in 1885 were anything but soldiers and patriots of the highest character, but if there is any difference it is in favour of the men who went around the world to carry the British flag to victory. Certainly we owe much to those who sacrificed everything for imperial senti-

ment. So far as we were concerned we were in no material danger. But there was danger to the empire which we uphold. These men did not stop to consider the cost to themselves, and we should not stop to consider the cost to ourselves now. When these men went out it was a matter of pride to Canada to pay their wages, and I think it should be ten times more a matter of pride to Canada to see that those soldiers who did her such honour on that occasion and rendered the empire such signal service, should not be dependent on the pittance of pension which is derivable under the British army regulations. That pension list is framed with regard to a certain class of people, to the ordinary soldiers of the British army. But the conditions of the Birtish army and of the class of people who serve in the ranks of the regular army, are different from those which prevail in this country, and amongst the men who served Canada and the empire so well in South Africa, and will be demeaning ourselves if we fail to recognize those fellow-countrymen of ours who did us "such great credit; if we fail to recognize their service in some more liberal fashion than we have done so far in leaving them entirely to the support of the British pension list. That would be leaving them without any recognition at all on our part. I believe that without distinction of party, without distinction of race or creed, or anything else, the people of this country will be proud to grant a liberal compensation to every soldier who has suffered physical disability in performing military service in South Africa.

I wish to say a few words merely to indicate my hearty concurrence in every word that has been uttered by the two hon. gentlemen (Mr. Broder) and (Mr. Oliver) who have spoken on this subject. Loyalty and defence of one's country are two of the highest qualities of citizenship, and those who are prepared in the hour of danger to expose and even give up their lives in defence of their country are in my judgment deserving of the highest recognition we can pay them. No reward is too high, no return too great that we can make for their services. It is a well known fact that all civilized countries deal generously with those who perform military service in defence of their flag, and those who have been maimed or have suffered physically while performing military duties have special claims upon our gratitude. The British empire is noted the world over for the care it takes of its defenders. In this country many lives of our valuable citizens have been sacrificed in our defence, many also have been sacrificed in defending the empire where our own country was not directly involved. In both cases I think our soldiers deserve the fullest gratitude of their countrymen. Those who were unfortunate enough to suffer as poor Trooper Mulloy suffered by los-457
ing his eyesight, should be especial objects of our commiseration, of our sympathy and our care, and our government should show substantial evidence of our gratitude for what Mr. Molloy has done. It seems to me that it is a crying shame that he should be allowed to go through life without a special compensation, with only the sixty-five cents a day allowed him by the British pension list, and nothing at all from Canada. Has it come to this, that in this enlightened age of the world the only proof we show of our admiration for loyalty, and for those who have endangered their lives and suffered physicial disability in the defence of their country, is the pittance allowed them by the British pension list, and that we in Canada are to do nothing more to mark our gratitude for our own fellow-citizens who have rendered us such signal service ? To my mind every man who went out to South Africa, whether he took part in active hostilities or not, if he went out in defence of the empire and in the maintenance of its authority, should be dealt with by us in the most liberal fashion, and we should be prepared to show in some very substantial wray our recognition of the very valuable services they have rendered to their country.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. A. GALLIHER (Yale and Cariboo).
speechtext:
I also desire to add a few words to what has been said by the hon. members who have spoken on this subject. I heartily concur in the remarks they have made. A number of men went out from my own district to the South African war, some of whom have returned and some of whom have lost their lives in that country. Among those who have returned there is now living in the town of Itossland a young man who was a very able "and efficient soldier and scout, and who went out both in the first and the second drafts. He has been practically disabled from the exercise of his ordinary calling in life by an accident in consequence of which the muscles of his left arm are withering. I think such a case deserves recognition at the hands of this government. The case mentioned by the hon. member for Dundas (Mr. Broder) is an exceptional case, and should be dealt with with exceptional generosity by this government. There are others whose services should also be recognized, although perhaps not as liberally.
I have no doubt that our government are fully alive to this question, and that they will deal liberally with these men who were so unfortunate as to have suffered in consequence of their loyalty, which impelled them to go forth to battle for the empire. There is another matter to which I wish to refer, and I feel a little delicacy in doing so for the reason that I myself was a member of the contingent w'hich went to Egypt and served in the campaign of 1884-5. While most of those who served in the rebellion of 1885 in Canada have received recognition by way of land grants from one or other of



the governments in Canada, no attention lias ever been paid to those who took part in the Soudan campaign of 1S84-5. If 1 were the only one concerned, I certainly would never mention it, but there are scattered throughout Canada many men who took part in that campaign, and I may say that they took a part that was creditable to themselves and creditable to Canada. They formed a very efficient corps of the British army engaged in the campaign of the Soudan. I think that while this question of recognizing the services of Canadians in South Africa is being and has been taken up by the government we should not forget those boys who served in an equally dangerous position, as any one knows who has run the cataracts of any waters, while at the same time being exposed to attack from the enemy. Their claim, I think, is one that should also be taken into consideration by the government. This is the first time I have mentioned it, and 1 think the occasion an opportune one to draw the attention of the government to the claim of these men, who, 1 think.it will be admitted, are deserving of some recognition.

I do not know that I can add anything to that which has been so well expressed by my hon. friend from Dundas (Mr. Broder) and other gentlemen who have spoken, but I desire to say that, as far as I am concerned, I would heartily support any appropriation by the government for the purpose of doing what I think is no more than justice to these men who have suffered from the service which they have rendered to the country in South Africa. The case of Mr. Mulloy may be taken as an illustration. I have no doubt there are other cases that are equally deserving. I had an opportunity of meeting Mr. Mulloy when he came to Halifax for the purpose of receiving some instruction at a school for the blind in that city. I may say that I induced him to tell me the story of the occasion on which he lost his eyesight, and although it was told with a very great deal of modesty and not putting himself forward in any way, I felt very much impressed by the ability and gallantry which he displayed on that occasion, and I regard him as a man who is .eminently deserving of consideration at the hands of the government for the way in which he served his country then. We hailed the departure of these men for South Africa with a great deal of satisfaction. They were acclaimed by crowds cheering them on their departure, and they were met with like receptions upon their return. Taking the case of Mr. Mulloy; he has been deprived of that blessing of sight, a loss which will render liis life altogether different in the future from what it would have been. He is a man of great ability, a man who could have looked forward to a distinguished career in this country ; he has lost that most precious boon of Mr. GALLIHER.
eyesight in the service of his country, he is now practically incapable of earning his livelihood, he is left in that condition by the country for several years, and not one single dollar has ever been contributed by the country for the purpose of supporting or maintaining him. I do not think this is a condition of affairs which ought to make us proud of this country, and the sooner it is remedied the better. I am aware that the question of pensions might open up a very wide scope if we do not proceed upon some definite principle, but the case of Mr. Mulloy and other men who have incurred disability in South Africa, it seems to me can be dealt with without any danger at all to the public interest. It will impose no great burden upon the country, and any precedent which is fixed by dealing generously with these men will not be a dangerous one. I would very heartily support any measure introduced by the government for the purpose of doing what, as I have said before, is no more than simple justice to these men.

The case of Private Mulloy, which has been brought to the attention of the House by my hon. friend from Dundas (Mr. Broder), is one which can not but excite the sympathy of every man who is familiar with it. Private Mulloy not only showed himself to be a good soldier in the field, but he has borne the great misfortune which he sustained in the loss of his eyesight, with a courage and a fortitude which excites the admiration of every one who has been made aware of it. I think that the case of Private Mulloy should not be taken up separately. If we are to deal with this question we ought to deal with it as a whole instead of dealing with the case of one or other of those who have in a greater or less degree suffered in consequence of the discharge of then-duty to their country. When the colonies were invited by the British authorities in October, 1899. to take their share in the war in South Africa, the British government undertook to defray certain expenses and undertook at the same time to deal with .the matter of pensions. The British government have discharged their undertaking in that behalf, but, according to our notions on this side of the Atlantic, a pension which perhaps might be found adequate in England seems to us strangely inadequate. A pension of 65 cents a day in Canada is not at all -what we would expect under similar circumstances. At the same time, I believe it is a fact that the patriotic fund which was raised in 1899-1900, and which, as I understand, reached a pretty high figure, has been made use of for the relief of those who. like Private Mulloy, have suffered in the South African war.

I do not know how much he got, but I am under the im-

pression that he received something. I refer to this now, not by way of putting a bar against the application of my bon. friend, but simply as a circumstance taken into consideration at the proper time. I can only say to my hon. friend that on a previous occasion I stated, speaking for the government, that I thought the country woidd respond to any action which might be taken by us if we were to undertake to deal generously with those who had risked their lives in the war. The matter has been engaging the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence (Hon. Sir Frederick Borden). I am sorry he is not present to-day. In the rush of business of this long session, I am sorry to have to admit that for my part the matter has escaped my attention. I am sure it has not escaped the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence and probably at some day-I cannot say when
I intimated to the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence that I would bring it up in the House, and he was therefore aware that I intended speaking upon it,

I do not find fault with that. The Minister of Militia is absent to-day for a very good reason, but if he were present, he could have given the conclusion which he has reached on the subject. I shall make it my duty to call his attention to the matter, and to point out the sympathetic reception it has received from the members of this House.

This is the third time this question has been brought before the House during the present session. It, however, was not in reference to this specific case of Private Mulloy, but with general reference to all those who have suffered disability in South Africa. ' I think tlie Prime Minister is right in saying that we cannot make Private Mulloy's case exceptional. I have had several interviews with the Minister of Militia and he has expressed himself as prepared to give a favourable consideration to the whole matter. I am pleased to hear the Prime Minister say that he endorses that idea. The approval of the hon. gentleman, of course guarantees its accomplishment. I would point out, that there are many who are partially disabled through the loss of an arm, a leg or one eye, and the money available from the patriotic fund is not at all sufficient to meet the requirements of these cases. I would remind the Prime Minister that, in addition to a moderate pension, these young gentlemen who are partially disabled could be employed in some suitable positions in the public service. In England, a society has been formed to get positions for army reserve men, and for those who have 'been partially disabled in war. and the employers of England are responding to the objects 457*
of the society in a very commendable mar. her. None of these young Canadians whc are partially disabled wish to avoid work, and I suggest now to the Prime Minister that positions might be found for them in the government service. The question of pensions generally, has engaged the attention of various nations. New Zealand has an efficient pension system not only for those who are disabled in the service of the empire, but for those who on account of old age are not able to work longer. The highest statesmen in England have proposed a scheme of old age pensions to be paid from the national resources. I believe that the Prime Minister will be endorsed by every member of this House if before the session closes, he will bring down an appropriation in the estimates to pay a pension to the comparatively few men who have been seriously disabled in the South African war. I aril delighted to know that my hon. friend (Mr. Gallilier) is one of the old Nile voyageurs, and I congratulate him on bringing the question of a land grant before the House. I trust that the government will give its careful attention to that matter. As an instance of the reasons which some people give for requiring a pension, I may say that an old gentleman came to me and told me that lie was out in '37 and '38, and he asked me to advance his claim. As a matter of fact he did'nt fight at all, but he had turned out for two days, and he thought lie was entitled to a pension. I asked him wbicli side he fought on, and he said he was on the side of the Loyalists, but I told him that his chances were better for getting some recognition, if he had supported the other side:	However that may be, this
nation should now turn its attention to compensating in some way, the men who have been disabled in the loyal defence of the empire. Probably there are not more than forty or fifty Canadians who have been permanently disabled in the late war, and I do not believe that one-thousandtli part of one per cent of the people of Canada would object to our granting these men pensions.

Could the hon. gentleman tell me whether any one of these soldiers who fought in South Africa has received compensation from the insurance fund that we heard so much about in the session of 1900 from Sir Charles Tupper, who then led the opposition V

I suppose at this date it is no harm to mention names, and I may state, that when I made an offer of troops for South Africa, Mr. Hugh Graham of the Montreal 'Star'-who has received so much attention to-day-wired me offering to pay an insurance of $1,000 on the life of each of the thousand men I was anxious to enrol. I understand, however, that this insurance was for loss of life ; I do not think it applied to disability.

14(300
I understand there was a scale of indemnity attached to it, which was to be granted for partial disablement.

I do not know about that. I was fortunately not compelled to draw upon any such fund, but even if this fund did give an indemnity to men who were disabled, I do not think any one in Canada would object to their receiving in addition some recognition from the state.
I know of two cases quite near my own home, where this insurance referred to by the bon. gentleman (Mr. Monet) was paid.
Were these men disabled ?
They were killed.

In view of the general expression of opinion from all sides of this House, and the sincere sympathy expressed by the right hon. Prime Minister, it is unnecessary to add anything further to what has been said on the question. I listened, however, with regret, to the statement of the Prime Minister, that there was practically no hope of this question being solved this session, which I understand is rapidly drawing to a close. As the right hon. gentleman says the question is still in the hands of his ministers, and therefore not under the consideration of the government, it seems almost hopeless to expect that it will be brought to an end and that any mature plan will be evolved by the government. Now, I do not interject that for the purpose of attempting to make capital against the government, but I do suggest that in view of this very general feeling in the House something ought to be done; I do suggest that an effort should be made to mature a plan that will work out a solution at once, instead of having the matter thrown over to be dealt with at the next session of parliament.

Reference has been [DOT]made by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes) to the desirability of giving employment to the South African veterans in addition to any financial aid which may be given. I think it is but fair to say that the government have acted in that direction. I can bear testimony to the fact that the ex-Minister of Railways has given employment on the Intercolonial Railway in the maritime provinces to a very large number of these men.

Mr. .1. T. SCHELL (Glengarry). Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair, I wish to rise to a question of privilege. When the House was in Committee of Supply, on Thursday last, the 13th, the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid), for the fourth time,

I believe, this session, again coupled my name with that of the superintendent of the Williamsburg canal. He had previously stated several times that this gentleman was an appointee of mine, in the course of some remarks not reflecting very favourably on the superintendent of the canal. I have just noticed that as reported on page 14147 of ' Hansard ' the hon. gentleman used these words :
As I mentioned the other night, when he was given this important position, one of the most important positions on the river, a position the occupant of which should know the marine interest thoroughly, he was a school teacher in Glengarry. I do not believe he over saw a canal before he was placed in this important position- he was the financial agent-I will put it mildly- of the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Schell).
I wish to state, Mr. Speaker,-and I wisii to put it mildly-that this statement is absolutely and entirely and unqualifiedly untrue. As I stated before, this Mr. Stewart was at one time, as a young man, a school teacher in Glengarry. Later he was employed in Montreal. Ottawa, and I cannot tell what other places, but during the year 1900 and for I do not know bow many years previous to that time, he was not a resident of Glengarry. He was not my financial agent, he was not an appointee of mine, I had no connection with Mr. Stewart. It is too had.' Mr. Speaker, that a member from his privileged position In this House, should go the length that the hon. member for Grenville did, even to attack a government employee. I know Mr. Stewart, and I understand from the department that lie is a good and capable oflicer, and even if he does not suit the member for Grenville, it is not a fair tiling that he should be attacked in this manner. I may say that Mr. Stewart Is not one of the Glengarry Stewarts ; he was not born in Glengarry, and so far as I know, is not related to the Glengarry Stewarts.
That is a good thing for them.

Mr. Speaker, probably no one statement ever made in the House of Commons has attracted more attention than the historical one made in the year 1S94 by the opposition of that day, that the revenue and expenditure of Canada should be kept at a point about $2,000,000 less than the $38,000,000 which was then the expenditure of the country. These gentlemen did not all agree as to the amount by which the $3S,000,000 might be reduced. Some wanted a reduction of $2,000,000 ; others $3,000,000 or $4,000,000 ; some $5,000,000 ; and I think one gentleman would have applied the pruning knife to the extent of $0,000,000. However, if we take $2,000.000 as the more moderate estimate and the more likely to be the correct one and apply that to the expenditure of that day, then, in the opinion of those critics, the ordinary expenditure of Canada ought to be $30,000,000, and its total expenditure, including expenditure on capital account, about $41,000,000. Practically, the promise was made to the people by the gentlemen then representing the Liberal party that if elected they would carry on the affairs of the country for the- sum I have just mentioned. No doubt the country did take these gentlemen seriously. No doubt the country understood that, if returned to office, they would reduce the expenditure of the country and the consequent taxation imposed on the people to something like the extent they promised. I need scarcely say that this promised economy has not been carried out. If we will regard the expenditure and income of Canada to-day from that point of view most readily understood, namely, the amount per capita, we will find that since 1 SPG the revenue, and consequently the taxation. of Canada has increased at a very rapid rate, and that the expenditure of the country has increased in proportion. Instead of the government realizing what the people expected, it has gone lin the very opposite direction. Instead of practicing economy it has gone on steadily increasing the burdens of the people and the expenditure of the country. In 189C the revenue per head was $7.20 and the expenditure $7.20. In 1902, which is the last year for which returns were submitted by the government, the revenue, instead of being $7.20, was $10.64 and the expenditure $9.30. instead of $7.26 per head.
The balance was on the right side.

Yes. Last year, taking the figures which we find in the ' Gazette,' the revenue was $11.94 and the expenditure $9.37. Again the balance is on the right
side, but there is a very large increase over the figures of 1896. The increase per head since that time is in revenue $4.74 and in expenditure $2.11 per head, so that while this country has had an abundant revenue- and we will have opportunity before I conclude my remarks of tracing the sources of that revenue and showing the manner in which it has been collected and pressed upon the people-the promise of economy has been absolutely set at naught. Instead of maintaining the expenditure at the point fixed by these hon. gentlemen when in opposition, that expenditure has been increased by $2.11 per head. This increase of expenditure has been steady since 1S9G. The ordinary expenditure of Canada has increased from $37,000,000 in 1S9G to $52,000,000 this last year. And the total expenditure has increased from $44,000,000 to $G4,-000,000. The expenditure has gone up every year since the present government has been in power. Even this last year, in which there was at one time some prospect of economy, the expenditure has increased by $500,000 over that of the preceding year, when it was abnormally large. By these figures we can determine the manner in which the expenditure affects the individual householder. Take the average family at five and a half persons, we find that in 1903 the revenue had risen to $G5.G7 per family, or $11.94 per head, and the expenditure to $51.54 per family, or $9.37 per head. Avery large increase, I need scarcely say, over the figures which were recorded as altogether too excessive by the critics of 1893-4, when the Conservatives were administering our affairs. AVe would perhaps get a better idea of the steady manner in which the present government has kept increasing the expenditure by taking a series of years and contrasting the seven- years from 1890 to 1896- the last seven years of Conservative administration-when the average ordinary expenditure was $37,000,000 and the average total expenditure was $42,000,000, with the subsequent seven years. When we contrast those years with the seven years of Liberal administration of this government, who have been endeavouring very unsuccessfully to carry out their pledges of economy, we find that in those seven years in which this government has been in power, the average ordinary expenditure has increased from $37.000,000 to $44,000,000, and the average total expenditure from $42,000,000 to $54,000,000, making an increase of $7,000,000 in the one case and $12,000,000 in the other. These increases are very large. In the case of ordinary expenditure they amount to about one-fifth of the sum fixed by the Liberal party as that required to carry on the business of the country.- These gentlemen went so far as to say that there was absolutely no justification for a larger expenditure. But it is argued by these gentlemen, when they have been challenged from time to time for their failure to make good their promises, that

there is something in the existing conditions which justifies this large expenditure. They say that if the expenditure is great so is the revenue, and that the country oau afford an expenditure in 1903-4 which it could not afford seven years ago. They insisted in 1894, not only that the taxation was too high, but that'it was oppressive. Well, if we are to judge the affairs of the country by the conditions of its finances, we will find that there is no reasonable ground for that contention. There was no failure, no difficulty whatever in acquiring the revenues required for the use of the country at that time. A very brief survey of the financial condition of Canada in 1894, when these gentlemen were most positive in expressing these strong views, will show that the country provided, without any excessive taxation or any very burdensome impost, all the money required to carry on its business.
For instance, in 1893 the expenditure on account of consolidated fund was $37,000.000 in round numbers, and the total expenditure $41,000,000. In that year the revenue was $38,000,000, or $1,000,000 in excess of the expenditure on account of consolidated fund. In 1804. the expenditure on account of consolidated revenue fund was $37,000,000, and the total expenditure $43,000,000. In that year the revenue was $36,000,000, or about $1,000,000 less than the expenditure on current account. This was a comparatively small deficiency, and one that could easily have been made up by slight additions to the taxation of the country. It was a deficiency moreover which was due to the fact that large deductions had been made, under the capable administration of the Finance Minister of that time, in the taxation imposed upon the country. On the whole, for the two years I have given there was a surplus of $180,000. So, evidently, expenditure and revenue were very nearly balanced in these years. The revenue per bead in 1893 was $7.73, and in 1894, $7.29, while the expenditure was, for 1893, $7.40, and for 1S94, $7.54. These figures show that under the system of financing at that time in vogue, matters were managed by the government so as to keep revenue and expenditure just about where they should be- that is at almost a perfect balance.
Now, it must further be observed that at that very time we had entered upon a period of depression, a depression which came to its climax in 1895. We were not, as now, in a period of expansion, of buoyant trade, hut were approaching the lowest point in one of those depressions which periodically visit all countries. Furthermore, it must be borne in mind in making a comparison of that tiipe and this, that the Finance Minister of that day had withdrawn the duties upon sugar and other articles, and so had relieved the people of taxation to an amount which was estimated, and I think accurately estimated to save to the Mr. BELL.
people in a few years $19,000,000. The great relief afforded to the people of Canada by that immense reduction in taxation accounts very readily for the fact that there were at that time certain small deficits. At present we have an utterly different state of affairs. And, as I have been able to show the fallacy of the argument of the Minister of Customs that the country was in such a position, in the years I have referred to, that they were warranted in reducing taxation anl the public debt and curtailing expenditure, so I think I can show that if the government is now in the enjoyment of large revenue, it is because we are not only enjoying all the advantages of a period of prosperity, one of those periods which we, in common with all the rest of the world enjoy from time to time; but because during all this period of expansion, of prosperity, of great volume of business and high prices, the government of the day has not followed a 'sound financial system, has not relieved the people of taxation that is unnecessary for the purposes of the country, but has maintained throughout this period of expansion taxes which could only be justified under some pressing necessity requiring the government to take from the citizen every dollar that he could spare for the purposes of the government. The present government has not diminished the duties as did the government of which Hon. George E. Foster was the Finance Minister during a period of expansion and great prosperity previous to 1893. On the contrary, coming into power as they did, in 1896. when we were entering upon the period of expansion, of buoyant financial conditions, that we have enjoyed since that time, they proceeded to add to the taxation which had been imposed by Mr. Foster in order to meet the requirements of the country during the hard years of depression. They not only retained the taxes imposed by Mr. Foster, but added to them, and added to them very largely, by imposing taxation upon articles which are of universal use, and, therefore, the articles which most readily respond to the call of the government for increased revenue. Since it came into power, this government, even at a time when the current of business was flowing strong, at a time when we were evidently entering upon a period of good times, increased the duties on sugar, increased the duties on tobacco and increased the duties on spirits, all articles which respond readily to the effort on the part of the government to secure increased revenue. And, not only did they impose those duties, but they have maintained them during their whole period or1 office, a period when the revenue of the country was sure to be large, trade being buoyant and the business resources of the country greater. During the last year, we find that from sugar, an article on which the people of Canada in the years when these hon. gentleman criticised the government paid a very small duty, this government

The large surpluses which the government have had, mean, of course, that large sums in excess of the ordinary expenditure of the country, and of the ordinary requirements of the country, are taken from the citizens by the government.
Now, that is not ordinarily held to be good financing. It has been held to be good financing that the government should pay its way, that the revenue of the country should equal its ordinary expenditure. But in order to maintain matters at a proper level, the capital expenditure of the country is the expedient which has been devised in order to relieve the citizens from an excessive burden of taxation and to prevent the necessity of the government taking from them a larger sum of money than is required to meet the ordinary expenditure of the country. Consequently, to my mind, and I think it ought to be evident to every one, sound financing consists in reducing the expenditure of the country to the lowest point consistent with an efficient administration of the affairs of the country, and at the same time reducing taxation to a point where the revenue will precisely equal ordinary expenditure. Ordinary expenditure should be economically made and kept at the lowest possible point, and the revenue of the country ought to be kept to a point which will precisely meet or slightly exceed that ordinary expenditure. Except living expenses, the ordinary expenses required to meet the administration of the government, to meet the regular everyday
requirements of the people, all other works ought to be paid for, not out of the surpluses, which are only produced by excessive taxation, but ought to be paid for by a system of capital expenditure by which the cost of those works will be spread over, not one, two or three years, but over the whole period during which those works will be available, and they will be gradually paid for by the people during- the years in which they have the advantage of those expenditures. In this way each year the country pays its ordinary expenses, and in addition, by means of sinking fund, it pays its proportion of the capital outlay for the extraordinary expenditure which the country is required to incur.
Now there is another reason which to my mind makes it clear that a system which enables a government to be .in the possession of large surpluses, and to claim credit for them is a most objectionable system. The state, if it is economically and fairly well governed, can always procure money, can borrow money a great deal cheaper than even a rich citizen, and, of course, very much cheaper than a poprer citizen ; and if money is required for capital expenditure, it seems to me it is better financing, and better for the government, and better for the country that the moneys required for extraordinary expenses of the country should be procured by borrowing, and should be repaid by a system of judiciously applied sinking funds, rather than that this expenditure should be made out of surpluses which can only be in the possession of the government in consequence of the taxation of the country for the time, being excessive. There is another objection to surpluses, and one which was urged very strongly and effectively by a gentleman who sat upon this side of the House in the years in which the Conservative party were in power-for during many years when the Conservatives were in power, they did have surpluses to their credit-and that was the fact that the possession of large revenues, the possession of surpluses, the possession of excessive revenues, has a great tendency to lead to extravagance. I do not think we need go very far in considering the estimates, not only of this year, but of the years that are past, to discover that there are reasons to believe that the people of this country have not very far to look in the pages .of these estimates to find that the result of large revenues in the hands of this government, has been to largely increase the expenditure, and to induce that exti-avagance which we had every reason to believe would result in the case of every government that has large surpluses in excess of its needs.
Now, there is another reason still, to my mind, why the taxation should be reduced to the point at which it would meet the ordinary expenditure of the country aud no more. There are in the country a certain number of people who have wealth, who

have money to spare, but it is a small class. There is a much larger class to whom money is of great value, who have no money to spare, and on the other hand are for the greatest part of the time in the market borrowing money. Under a system that, without any process of taxation, derives large revenues from that portion of the population which has surplus funds, which has money to spare, we find that in addition to other sums which the present government have borrowed, they have in their hands, and are using, nearly $100,000,000 which were loaned to them practically by the people of this country. They have nearly $40,000,000 of notes in circulation, pieces of paper with the endorsement and guarantee of the government upon them, which are accepted by the people as cash, and for which, of course, the government receives the equivalent of cash. To that extent the whole amount of the circulation of this country, which is nearly $40,000,000, is practically a loan made by the people to the government of the day. Then in the Dominion government savings bank and the postal savings bank of the country there are deposits of some $60,000,000 as well. From that class of people, from the business people who keep the money in circulation, and from the more wealthy people, who use the savings banks as banks of deposit-it is evident that the government to-day is receiving from that class, which has a superfluity and can spare, something like $100,000,000. They receive that at a very low rate of interest, the average interest upon that whole sum is only a fraction under 2 per cent; about i :87 per cent, I think. Now from these facts it seems clear that the government having $100,000,000 practically in their hands, have already withdrawn from circulation and from the coffers of those who can spare, of those who have money which they do not require, as large a sum of money as can be safely and advantageously contributed to the government by the people. When the government of the day maintains taxation at such a point that it is in a position to point to surpluses such as we have this year, an enormous surplus, then to my mind, the government of the day has taken from the pockets of the people, who require it more than they do, and can use it to better advantage than' they can, a large sum of money which would be far better in the pockets of the people than in the coffers of the government. Apart altogether from the fact that a large surplus at the hand of the government over and above what is required for ordinary expenditure, leads to extravagance, apart altogether from that, it is withdrawing from the pockets of the people a sum of $14,000,000 this year, which the country could use to much better advantage than can the government. A great part of the people of this country are borrowers, as a rule they have to pay 6 or 7 per cent for the money which they borrow.
