That in addition to the sums so voted large increases of the public expenditure have been made which are authorised by statute to be paid out of consolidated fund. Among these are railway subsidies ov.er thirteen million dollars.
That this House desires to place on record the opinion that the expenditure for the year
1903	and the proposed expenditure for the year
1904	are excessive and extravagant, and that it views with alarm the course of the government towards ever-increasing expenditure, its failure to reduce the public debt by maintaining a high rate of taxation, and its adding to capital expenditure and to the obligations of the country enormous sums for whiih the country cannot receive adequate returns.

Whatever difficulties we may have with respect to economy in other matters, I think we have reached the stage in the business of the session when we'can all agree that economy of speech is desirable. Therefore though my hon. friend from Pietou (Mr. Bell) has covered a very considerable ground-I will not say at much length-and has referred to many questions which would tempt one to occupy time, I
shall deem it necessary to condense my remarks as much as possible, and, for that reason, to deal only with what I regard as the chief points. I think my hon. friend labours under a great difficulty, which is common to all hon. gentlemen on that side. Thesp hon. gentlemen seem to be utterly unable to appreciate the changes which have come over this country since the days of 1896 with which they make comparisons. Perhaps it is not unnatural that they should experience that difficulty. When we recall the predictions they made as to the dreadful things that would happen to this country if a Liberal government should come into power, and when we recall what has happened since that day ; when we contrast the reality with the predictions of my hon. friends : when we realize that the public appreciate the great change that has taken place, perhaps we should allow hon. gentlemen the privilege of still shutting their eyes to the great facts which are apparent to the public at large. I would like to say to my hon. friend that the speech he has made and the resolution he has moved would he alarming, if we had not had a number of such speeches and a number of such resolutions in previous years towards the close of the several sessions under Liberal rule. I remember that in the first session in which the Liberal government took charge of affairs, in 1896, the distinguished gentleman who then occupied the position of the leader of the opposition, in a very eloquent and vigorous address declared that it was a moral certainty that the government would come out at the end of the fiscal year with a most disastrous showing, that they would have a deficiency of some $3,000,000. At the end of the year the deficiency proved to be a very modest one-some five hundred odd thousand dollars if my memory serves me well. And every session since that time, we have had one of these alarmist speeches, and one of these alarmist resolutions, in which all the moneys we have voted have been rolled up into one great sum with a view to persuading the people that, under the financial legislation of the session, nothing but disaster could come upon this afflicted country. But somehow or other, when the end of the year has been reached and the accounts have been made up, the people have discovered that the finances of the country have prospered, that these dreadful things have not happened, that the world has moved on in a very nice and comfortable way, and that Canada, instead of being obliged^ to face deficits, as in the past has enjoyed an era of very comfortable surpluses. And so, 1 venture to say the citizens of Canada, reminded as they will be of these dreadful speeches and dreadful anticipations of former times, will understand that the speech made and the resolution moved to-night by my hon. friend from Pietou is only another I one of these alarms which they are not just-

ified in talcing too seriously. Hon. gentlemen opposite have been crying out these alarms year after year and session after session, so they must not be surprised if the people no longer take much stock in them.
I do not attempt to deny the apparent fact that the expenditure of this country has grown very largely since 1896. But it has grown for good and proper purposes. Instead of apologizing for that expenditure, we are proud to refer to it, because that expenditure, we believe, has been one of the instrumentalities which have brought about the growth and the progress of the country since 1896. The growth and progress and prosperity of Canada for the last few years, undoubtedly, have come from the industry, intelligence, energy and thrift of the people. But all these qualities would have been vain if they had not beeen assisted by wise legislation ; and we believe that this government and this Liberal party, by their financial legislation as well as by other measures, by the liberality and wisdom of their public expenditure, have been doing much to help the people to produce the splendid results which the records of the country jilace before them.	-
We have spent more money. Let me take a few of the principal classes of our expenditures as compared with 1890. We spent last year $846,345 more on militia than was spent in 1890. Is there any lion, gentleman opposite who objects to that " expenditure ? Do not we know that, far from opposing the militia expenditure, there has been a tendency on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite to demand larger expenditures on this service ? Do not we know that, again and again suggestions have been made by these hon. gentlemen with regard to the militia of the country which would involve us in very large expenditures ? So,
I may fairly ask my hon. friends opposite to agree with me that, in that great item where we have spent almost $1,000,000 more than in 1S96, there is no room for criticism. We expended in 1903 on public works about $2,750,000 more than was spent in 1890. Sir, these expenditures have covered the whole face of the Dominion, and they have been wise and useful expenditures. It would be foolish for any of us to claim that, in Ihe expenditure of so much money from ocean to ocean, employing a vast army of officials and servants, every man engaged has been absolutely faithful to a cent ; it would he foolish to say that in no case had a mistake been made ; it would be foolish to say of the men employed in public affairs, any more than of men employed in private affairs, that all are perfect. But. take it all in all, I do not hesitate to say in the light of all the inquiries that have been made, that these expenditures on public works have been wise and useful expenditures, and have been instrumental in helping on the progress and prosperity of the country. We Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
spent on the lighthouse and ocean service of Canada $498,000 in 1903 more than was spent in 1S96. Shall we apologize for that expenditure before the people of Canada today ? No. Are we not a great maritime country ? Have we not our great waterway, the St. Lawrence, which must be improved with buoys, lights and all the various aids to navigation 1 Have we not our coast line in Quebec and the maritime provinces, as well as in, British Columbia, where we must have lighthouses and all the other improvements which protect the mariner ? We have been expending money for these services ; and, far from regretting it, far from apologizing for it, we say that in face of criticism such as hon. gentlemen have offered tonight that we are prepared to provide the money and do the work, and let the world know that our national highway is a highway of safety for the commerce of nations. We spent $100,000 more on the fishery service in 1903 than we spent in 1896. Shall we. apologize for that ? Is there a man in this House who does not recognize the importance of the great fishing industry of this country ? Is there one who does not recognize the obligation resting upon us to nourish and encourage and protect that Industry ? We have spent more money, and, no doubt, as the days roll on, the minister in charge of that great department will find it necessary to spend still more ; and, if he is able to spend it with the same justification as can be given for ,the expenditure in the past, we shall not need to apologize before tbe people of Canada for that use of their money. We spent on tlie service of immigration in 1903. $52G,000 more than was expended in the year 1896. Shall we, in the face of what we have seen in the west, apologize before this House for that increased expenditure ? The little that hon. gentlemen opposite spent in 1896 accomplished nothing. Every dollar that has been expended in the immigration service of this country under the present administration has brought a rich harvest for the present and will bring a richer harvest for the future of Canada.
My hon. friend from Pictou says that in that respect there "is an exodus from the lower provinces. We have discussed that question before, and I say to my hon. friend that there is, there has been for a great many years, and I imagine there always will be, some movement of population from those provinces. They, are an adventurous people who live by the seaside, their tendency is to go abroad, and I do not expect tbe time will ever arrive when that movement will not be found to some extent. But I do take the responsibility of saying to-day that throughout tbe lower provinces there is a better condition in that respect than there has been at any other time during tbe last quarter of a century. I say there are fewer people leaving the maritime provinces, and I say that in most parts of the maritime

provinces the question to-day is not one of an exodus, the question is to find men to labour on the works which are opening up all over these provinces.
We have spent $565,000 more in connection with our sinking fund. That is a mere matter of book-keeping, it adds nothing to the burden of the country, it is an assistance to the redemption of the public debt, and whether it be large or small, it is practically a provision for redemption, and our obligations are not in any sense increased. We have spent more money on the administration of justice-my hon. friend called attention to that. I have not the figures he used, but it is a curious thing for my bon. friend to select that as the subject of complaint, when we have ill our mind the fact that only a few days ago, when there was a discussion in this House with regard to the salary of judges, almost without exception every hon. gentleman who rose on the other side asked that the salaries of the judges be increased. What is the use of the hon. gentleman standing up and denouncing an expenditure when he knows that the general feeling of the men around him is rather in favour of increasing that expenditure than of reducing it ?
We spent last year on the item of the customs service, $332,000 more than in 1890. I have no doubt that hon. gentlemen op posite will go throughout the country and will point to the fact that under the administration of my hon. friend the Minister of Customs the expenditure has increased to that extent ; but they will forget to mention the fact that by means of that increased expenditure of $332,000, he is able to show an increase in the revenue of $17,170,000. There was an increase in the expenditure in connection with excise of a little more than $8,000 last year, as compared with 1896 ; but that slightly increased expenditure was incurred in th* machinery for collecting a revenue which increased to the extent of $4,087,000. We spent last year on expenditure chargeable to the consolidated fund on account of the post office, $440,000 more than in 1896 ; but on the other side of the account, which hon. gentlemen are careful not to mention, the revenue was increased by $1,443,000. We increased the working expenses of the Intercolonial-practically they were doubled-we increased them about $3,184,000, but every dollar of that increased expenditure in the working of tlie Intercolonial, apart from the capital account, came back to us in something more than a dollar in the increased revenue which came from the road.
My hon. friend, in presenting his bill of alarm, magnified the figures of the railway subsidies as much as ihe could, and he made, not for the first time this session, the statement that these subsidies have been brought down at the end of the session when there is not time to consider them. I have taken the trouble to look into the record of the
former government on that question, and I find that beginning with the year 1885, there never was a single occasion in the history of the Conservative government when these railway subsidies were brought down as early as they have been in the present session. These subsidies were placed on the notice paper of the House of Commons on October 6. I suppose, if things move prosperously, we may look forward to what the Prime Minister sometimes describes as the blessings of prorogation, at the end of the present week. Assuming that we shall close on Saturday next, though 1 hope it will be Friday, I want to point out that there will then be eighteen clear days from the time these subsidies were brought down until it is contemplated parliament will prorogue. Compare that with what happened in the days of the Conservative administration. I find that in 1894 they brought their railway subsidies down five days before the session closed ; in 1893, five days before the session closed ; in 1890, four days before the session closed ; in 1887, three days before the session closed ; and in the *whole record of all these years, the longest period that they ever allowed for the consideration of the railway subsidies-and that was in one year only-was a period of twelve days. So I am able to say to my hon. friends that they have no cause of complaint with regard to the manner in which these subsidies have been brought before the House. This has been a busy session. It is not the business of the government to load down the Order Paper with a vast amount of business that cannot be digested by the House ; it is the business of the government to keep the House supplied fully with leading and important measures, and there never has been a session of parliament in which that duty has been better performed than it has been by this government during the present session.
My hon. friend deals with these railway subsidies as if they were to be expended all in one year. He does not say that, but the manner in which his speech is framed and his resolutions are framed, will convey the impression, I am afraid, as it has in the past, that the sums mentioned will all be expended in one year. Now my hon. friend knows and will admit that that would be a very erroneous impression.
Ml-: BELL. I think I stated that these would not be all expended in one year. Perhaps the hon. gentleman did not notice that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext:
Then the question arises, why they should be included in dealing with the expenditure for one year, for my hon. friend realizes that these subsidies in some cases will never be expended at all. The experience of the past is that some companies which come forward and induce the government to grant these subsidies, come forward in good faith,

find that they cannot finance the undertaking. In some cases it has happened in the past, that the amounts have not been paid at all. That will no doubt happen in some cases in the present instance ; but even in cases where these railways are undertaken it will take several years to construct them, and this vast sum of money which my hon friend includes in his bill to frighten the citizens of Canada, will, so far as it becomes payable at all, cover a number of years. In answer to a question put in the House a few days ago, I was able to state that in the term of ten years the subsidies granted to the various lines of railway, approximated-because as respects some of them, you cannot fix the exact amount to $27,000,01)0 ; yet the actual figures of expenditures show that during those ten years the payments for subsidies only amounted to $15,000,000. So if we follow the experience of the past and strike a fair average, what we shall probably have to pay, taking one year with another, will be about $1,500,000 each year in railway subsidies. That will not be an excessive sum when we consider the splendid territory it will develop, and the disposition that is manifest now from ocean to ocean to take up new enterprises with more courage and more hope than ever existed in former years.
But, Sir, I observe that my hon. friend, while contenting himself with these general denunciations, does not attempt to indicate any particular item, either in the railway subsidies or in any other portion of our public expenditure, with which he can find fault. I should perhaps make an exception, because he has mentioned one or two items- I do not remember the exact figures, I suppose altogether $15,000 or $20,000 for two public works. But at whatever sum my hon. friend may place them, where does he find himself then ? We have appropriations which run up to, I think he said, $200,000,000 or more. My hon. friend has the figure, but, whatever it is, he has not ventured to move to strike out any of those items, but he stands up and denounces them generally. I think he said it is $200,000,000 or more.
More than that.

But, whatever it is, he has not ventured to move to strike out any of these items, but he stands up and denounces them all generally. He may say that as respects the transcontinental railway he did record his vote against it, but he did so at the same time that his leader brought forward another scheme that everybody knows was more expensive than the one that we proposed. If my hlon. friend goes back to the grand old county of Pictou, talks as he has talked to-night and denounces these railway subsidies, one can imagine an old Scotchman standing up and saying :	My friend, did you vote against
them ? No. Why didn't you ? You moved

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
a resolution that this expenditure was extravagant, that the country was alarmed- why did you not record your vote ? My hon. friend will probably say : I could not very well do that, because some of these subsidies were going down into my own county. That would be all right, if my hon. friend would only take a broad-minded view of the matter. He knows that these subsidies are voted for his own county for useful and necessary works. In the vast territory which we have in Canada, no one man or set of men can have a knowledge of affairs from ocean to ocean which will enable them to judge of the requirements in the different provinces of Canada. But every section of this Dominion is represented in this House, and each group of members has its own local knowledge of its own province, so that it is possible for hon. gentlemen opposite to obtain a general idea of the wisdom or unwisdom of these expenditures. I feel quite sure, from what I know of the hon. member for Pictou, that if he thought that these expenditures were unwise, alarming, rash and extravagant, as he says in his 1'esolution, he would not be content with vague denunication, but he would move to strike the objectionable items out. True, my hon. friend asks : What is the good of doing that since we will vote vote against it? Yet that does not prevent my hon. friend from moving this resolution that we are probably going to vote against it. We have this vain, indefinite, academic resolution, which means nothing and leads to nothing. Unless my hon. friend is prepared to move a practical resolution, which would strike out a railway appropriation, or the appropriation for some great public work, I am afraid that the House and the country will not attach very much importance to the resolution which lie has moved. I am quite sure that the astute, intelligent people of Canada, not only in his province, but in all the other provinces, will say that when hon. gentlemen opposite take that ground they cannot be very serious in their denunciations of this lavish expenditure. But, Sir, if economy is desirable, and if it is not to be obtained from this government, where are the afflicted people of Canada to obtain it ? From hon. gentlemen opposite ? The wildest dream of the most unreasonable person in this Dominion would never expect a policy of economy from a Conservative government. From time immemorial they have declared for economy, but they have not practiced it and they do not even practice it now. Hon. gentlemen opposite know that I am calling their attention to a simple truth when I say tihat in nine cases out of ten when they rise to discuss some public expenditure, it is for the purpose of asking that the government do something on a more liberal scale than we have been doing in the past. We ask them, as we have done in the past, to point out anything that is wasteful or extravagant. They cannot do it. Usually the Public Accounts Committee

is the body that investigates these things. I venture to say that never in the history of this Dominion was there such a farce as the meetings of the Public Accounts Committee during the present session. We could not get the hon. gentlemen to attend. They used to come and introduce a motion that somebody be summoned, they would give notice that they intended to move to inquire into something, but when the time came for them to make the motion, they would not be there, or they had not called the witness, or something else would happen, and really the thing became laughable in the end. The Public Accounts Committee adjourned, and there was practically no inquiry into the public accounts of the past year. Why ? Not because hon. gentlemen opposite were not able, not because they were too generous to avoid an inquiry in the expenditures of the government, but simply and solely because they found there was no ground for attacking the expenditures of the government. I have said that if economy is not to be expected on our side there is very little prospect of it from hon. gentlemen opposite. I do not know a case in which hon. gentlemen opposite have advocated economy. We brought down what we' thought to be a wise proposal in reference to a great transcontinental railway. Hon. gentlemen opposite were not content to simply negative that, but they had to bring forward a policy of their own, which certainly could not have the merit of being more economical than the one the government proposed. We have a provision on the statute-book authorizing us to spend $750,000 for a fast Atlantic line, and we have been looking for somebody to do the work for this appropriation. Hon. gentlemen opposite stand up and move a resolution scoffing at the idea of our being able to get a fast Atlantic service for $750,000 a year, and telling us that we must get a fast line, cost what it will. Then, in order to make the thing if possible a trifle more ridiculous than that, about three-quarters of the hon. gentlemen opposite have been complaining of this government because we have not sent our good friend Captain Bernier to hunt up the north pole.
There is where you made a mistake.

There is a good consistent old Conservative. He is going to vote for this resolution declaring that the expenditures are alarming, and he is going to ask the government to spend a couple of hundred thousand dollars to send Captain Bernier to the north pole. Let him go through the record of the public service, and he will find that a suggestion of economy never comes from the side of hon. gentlemen opposite. Again and again we have heard complaints made that this government is not. dealing with sufficient liberality. The words of the hon. member for 458
Colchester (Mr. Gourley) are still ringing in our ears. My hon. friend from Pictou denounces as extravagant the railway subsidies which we brought down, and which we thought were fair and moderate. But the hon. member for Colchester made the declaration that they were paltry subsidies, and that if we had any respect for ourselves and for the country we would have brought down larger and more generous subsidies. My hon. friend simply expresses the general view of hon. gentlemen opposite. They move resolutions for economy, but they are vastly more extravagant than any hon. members who sit on this side of the House.
Let us look a little at the expenditures of the past. My hon. friend from Pictou has called attention to a fact, which we all know, that the expenditures during the years prior to 1S9C were much lower than they are now. Therefore, he assumes, because the expenditures were lower than they are now that theirs is a policy of economy and that ours is a policy of extravagance. Well, I do not think that is good logic. I think it is quite possible that a small sum might be spent in such a way as to constitute extravagance and that a large sum may be so spent as to constitute wise economy. It depends on whether you have the money to expend. That is a very vital matter. In the years 1894-5-6, when the economical government that my hon. friend is so anxious to praise were in power, although they spent less money than we did, they spent more money than they had to spend, and they added to the public debt. In 1894 they spent 103 per cent of their revenues. I am confining myself to what is called consolidated revenue fund. In 1895 they spent 112 per cent, or 12 per cent more than they had to spend, and in 1896 they spent a little more than 100 per cent-about 101 per cent. My hon. friend thinks that is economy. The fact is that, though we spent a great deal more money, we have the excuse that we had the money to spend. In 1897 we spent 101 per cent. That was the year during which the Liberal government did not have full control over the finances of the country. They came into power after the fiscal year had begun. They had to deal with the estimates prepared by their predecessors, and they did not have that full grasp of the finances of the country which they were able to obtain in later years, so that their expenditure for that year was a little more than their income; But in the following year, when the Liberals began to get their hands on the helm, we find that in the year 1898 this government spent only 95 per cent of its revenue ; in the year 1899 this government spent only 89 per cent of its revenue ; in the year 1900 this government spent only 84 per cent of its revenue ; in the year 1901 this government spent 89 per cent of its revenue ; in the year 1902 this government spent 87 per cent of its



revenue ; and in tlie year 1903, which has just closed, we spent 78 per cent of our revenue, as against the 101 per cent that the Conservative party spent in 1896. And yet the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bell) would have the country believe that, compared with the expenditure in 1896, our expenditure for the year 1903 was extravagant.
There is another way of viewing this matter. Let us take the public debt. After all these resolutions year after year from the opposition, as to the enormous obligations we are assuming and the enormous additions we are making to the public debt; the country would be prepared I suppose for a moderate increase per capita in the public debt. If I had to acknowledge that we had added two or three dollars per head to the debt of the people of Canada, it would not be anything that one need be ashamed of in view of the tremendous improvements which have been carried on during the past few years. But what are the facts ? In the year 1896 the net public debt stood at $50.96 per head ; in the year 1902 under a Liberal government, the net debt had fallen to $49.97, and in the year 1903, just closed, the public debt had fallen to $47.37 per head. Now, part of this decrease in 1903 is due to the readjustment of the accounts between the provinces and the Dominion, and therefore I do not take credit for it all; but if you make allowance for that you will And that even deducting that, "the net public debt of the Dominion stands to-day $47.97 per head as against $50.96 per head in the year 1896. That statement will surprise some of my hon. friends; it will surprise many people in this country who in consequence of such speeches as we have heard to-night, in consequence of such resolutions as the one now before the House, have been led into the impression that there is an enormous increase in the public debt of Canada.
I am glad to be able to say that as respects the year just closed, we have the most gratifying condition of affairs that it has ever fallen to the lot of a Finance Minister to announce. I have given the figures for the past year already, but I may be pardoned for giving them again. The revenue for the year 1903, ending June 30tli last, was $66,034,108.32; the expenditure of the ordinary character chargeable to the consolidated fund, was $51,707,172.89 showing a surplus of $14,326,935.43.
Hear, hear.

I repeat that the expenditure chargeable to consolidated fund, what is called the ordinary expenditure was $51,707,172.89; the charges to capital account, including all things charged to capital, were $10,367,163.01, making the total expenditure for the year $02.074,335.90. Now, in connection with this surplus, my hon. friend (Mr. Bell) had something to say about our charging bounties

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: to capital account, and he told us that in former times these bounties were charged to income. The fact is that in former times they were charged in such a mysterious way, that it was very hard to find them at all. They took the very curious form of a refund of duties. One would think that the common sense view is that a refund of duties is the paying back of money which has been paid, and how in the world the payment of a bounty which had never come into the treasury could properly be classified as a refund of duties, is one of these things which no fellow can understand. In former times, the Customs Department paid out of its receipts these bounties and thus reduced the customs revenue to that extent, which was a very curious method of bookkeeping.
Was it not after all paid out of consolidated fund, while the hon. gentleman charges it to capital ?

, Yes; it reduced the customs duties to that extent. That system continued because attention was not especially drawn to it, until the rearrangement of the Bounty Act, when we saw that we were going to pay very large sums in bounties. The sums that - were paid by the late government for iron and steel bounties, in proportion to the gross business of the country, were not in reality large; they did not affect the question of revenue, or expenditure, or surplus in any large degree. When, under the new condition of things, we found that large sums, running into the millions, were going to be paid for these bounties, we came to the conclusion that the old method of dealing with them was a mistake. Every business man in the House will say now, that whether they were charged to income or capital, the method of deducting them from the customs duties and treating them as a refund of duties, was unbusiness-like and improper. But, inasmuch as the bounties were based upon a sliding scale, contemplating their extinction in a short time, it was deemed well to charge them to capital account. In every financial statement I have presented to this House, I have invariably called attention to that point so that there could be no misunderstanding. I want to say, and it is notably so in this case, that whether you charge that to income or to capital, it would not have affected the general result, it would not have affected it perceptibly last year, because the income which was collected last year was sufficient to pay, and did pay all the ordinary expenditure of the country chargeable to consolidated fund, all the expenditures for bounties, all the expenditures for railway subsidies, all the expenditures for railway construction, all the expenditures of every shape and form were paid for last year out of the revenue of the country, and there was a large reduction in the public debt besides.
Hear, hear.

There was a decrease of the public debt on the operations of last year of $6,580,360.88; there was a further decrease in connection with the readjustment of the provincial accounts- and I have purposely separated the two-amounting to $3,305,450.24; making a total decrease in the net public debt of Canada at the close of the year as compared with the previous year, of $9,885,811.12.
Hear, hear.

I am glad to be able to say that the outlook for the business of the current year is in most respects entirely satisfactory. We do not want to rely too much on the future. I quite realize that the time may come when business may not be as brisk as it has been in the past, but for the present, the outlook is by no means discouraging. I am glad to be able to say that for the new fiscal year, from the first of July up to the twentieth of October (yesterday), the revenue for that period, as compared with the revenue of the corresponding period last year, shows a handsome increase of $2,620,000.
If my hon. friend's financial showing is so very good, why is it that he is unable to borrow money in London to-day at less than 4* per cent, when we could borrow it a few years ago at 3 per cent ?

The government of Great Britain have paid, I am told, 4rh pier cent for their money within the last month. My hon. friend is shutting his eyes to facts which the financial world understands, which the government of England understands and has to recognize. I have some difficulty in understanding the attitude of my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Bell) on the question of surpluses. For some years efforts have been made by hon. gentlemen opposite to prove that there were no surpluses, that thiey were a delusion, and indeed, before the hon. gentleman had concluded his speech, he got back to the old ground and began to argue that this surplus was not, after all, a real surplus. The bulk of his argument was that we have very large surpluses and we should not have them, that it is bad financing, and that we should reduce taxation. Will my hon. friend tell me on what ai'ticles he will reduce taxation ? The great policy of hon. gentlemen opposite is to increase taxation. Every motion that they have made on the fiscal policy has been in the direction of higher duties, and if called upon to reduce taxation they would find themselves in a difficult position to discover an article on which they are willing to have the duty reduced. Does the hon. gentleman want the duty on sugar reduced? I will not press the question.

I think, under the circumstances, with such a surplus as the gov-458*
ernment has, it would be quite warrantable to reduce the duty on articles of general consumption.

I understand that my hon. friend, speaking in the name of the opposition, says that the duty should be reduced on sugar.. But the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) says the duty on sugar should be increased for the benefit of the beet sugar industry. Now, if hon. gentlemen opposite are protectionists, if they want to encourage home industry, if they want to help the beet sugar industry, why do they want to cut down the measure of protection which the beet sugar industry already enjoys ? The hon. member for East Grey, in a former debate, said that they did not want to increase the duty, but only to have a bounty, but since that we have had the declaration again and again by hon. gentlemen opposite that a bounty is not the right way to aid an industry, that the true and only way to aid a home industry is by increasing the customs duties. Thus, if my hon. friend from Pictou speaks in the name of the Conservative party when he advocates the reduction of the duty on sugar be will have a difficult account to settle with the constituents of some of my hon. friends who' have sugar factories in their constituencies.
What is your attitude?

My attitude is disclosed in the budget speech and in the tariff as it stands. My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Bell) says we should not keep on these high taxes. Sir, this taxation is not so oppressively high. He falls into the error of assuming that because there is a great revenue there a great burden of taxation. The true way to look at that is that, so great has been the prosperity, so improved has been the purchasing x>ower of the people, that they have been able to consume all the products of our industries and to import many millions' worth from abroad, and in that way the revenue from customs has been greatly increased. But the customs tariff of this country in regard to most of the great staples, in so far as there has been any change at all, has been reduced. That is what hon. gentlemen opposite complain of; they complain that we are reducing the duties, yet my hon. friend says we are increasing the taxation. At one moment we are told that we are cutting down the duties and destroying the industries of the country and the next moment we have my hon. friend declaring that we are keeping the duties at too high a point.
Then he said that we should not charge these great works which we are carrying on now to income; they should be charged to capital: that, he said, is the very purpose of a capital account; raise just enough money to pay ordinary expenditure, and1 charge the balance to capital account. That would

be sound reasoning if you bad a tariff which was a burden to the people ; then if you raised money enough for ordinary expenditures and had to pay a great deal on capital account for great public works that course could be well justified. But why should you add to your capital account when it is not necessary? The complaint of hon. gentlemen opposite half the time Is that we are adding to the capital account more than we should. Did not my hon. friend (Mr. Bell), even before he concluded his own speech, complain that we are adding and charging too much to our capital account ? But, Sir, if you look at these figures you will find that the tariff and the taxation are not a burden. I will make the statement that the people of this country are not today complaining of undue taxation. I will state that, except perhaps on a few items the tariff is giving good satisfaction generally. The complaints we receive are not that the taxation is too high, but that the taxation is not high enough, and these complaints come from our friends opposite. Why should we go on charging things to capital account when we can provide for a large portion of .them out of revenue under a tariff . policy which is not burdensome V We can collect these large sums from year to year, and we have been able to provide for our ordinary expenditure and for a good portion of our capital account out of our income. We do not think we have charged anything to capital account which is not legitimate; but we were not prepared, in view of all that has been said for the last three or four sessions, for the sudden right about face which my hon. friend took to-night, when he spent fifteen minutes in condemning us because we did not charge more to capital account. What is the reason of our being able to charge these things to our income account ? We have been able to avoid going into debt to a degree which would otherwise be necessary, and by avoiding going into debt we avoid also the increase of interest charges. My hon. friend made some references to the increased charges for the public debt. I have here a statement showing the outlook for the present year with regard to1 our interest on the public debt. My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Bell) laboured under the difficulty that he was unable to take into account the great changes that have come over this country since 1896.
The hon. gentleman claims a saving from the adjustment of accounts between Ontario and the Dominion, but it is a mere book-keeping matter.

No, it is an absolute sum placed to the credit of the Dominion. It is a readjustment of the provincial account, and it is so much money less to be paid by the Dominion. My hon. friend should take into account the great change whicli has come over this country since 1896. The Canada of that day was vastly different from the Canada of today. The population of the Canada of that day was 5,086,061. We have not the exact population of to-day, we 'have to take it approximately, but a proper approximate statement is 5,528,847. The increase in population is not so great as we would like, hut in that respect we are making up for lost time, and the population is likely to increase much more rapidly than formerly. In 1890 we received 16,835 immigrants. In 1903 we received 128,364. In 1896 we had a revenue on consolidated fund of $36,618,590. In 1903 that revenue amounted to $66,034,108. In the year 1896, there were sales of public lands in Manitoba, the North-west Territories and British Columbia, to the amount of $93,303. In 1903, the sale of these lands represented $313,960. The total imports in the year 1890 were $118,011,508. In 1903,

under the great progress and prosperity of the country, at a time when our factories were busy and our people employed as never before in the history of the Dominion, the purchasing power of the people had so increased that they consumed more home produce and increased their imports from $118,011,508 to $241,214,961. The total exports in 1890 were $121,013,852, and in 1893 they amounted to $225,849,724. Our exports of home products, which perhaps is the better test of the prosperity and the activity of our people, amounted in 1896 to $109,915,337, and in 1903 they increased to $214,401,674. Our exports of products of the farm and animals and their products in 1896 amounted to $55,378,407, and in 1903 they were $114,441,863. Then take the article of manufacture, the very industry that lion, gentlemen opposite have tried to make themselves the special patrons of, which they claim the particular credit of nursing and nourishing. In 1896 our exports of manufactured products amounted to $10,222,S77 and last year they amounted to $20,624,967. The total trade of this country, which in 1896 was only $239,025,360, increased last year to $467,064,685. But though my hon. friends opposite seem unable to open their eyes to this vast change, the people of this Dominion are not so blind. The great mass of the people see these things, not only by the evidence of statistics, but by the evidence of the hum of industry which prevails almost in all parts of the Dominion, and they know that in this changed condition a very liberal expenditure is necessary. I remember on one occasion when my right hon. friend the Prime Minister was on a tour through the province of Ontario, observing in one of the very beautiful villages which was decorated for the event, a streamer stretched across the main street showing these words : ' Wise expenditure is true economy.' There was philosophy in that. There is a misunderstanding in some quarters as to what this economy means. Parsimony is not economy. It was not economy in 1894-5 and 6 to spend more money than we had, and it is not extravagance to-day for this government to spend a great deal less money than they are collecting. There is a policy that scatteretli and yet increaseth, and there is a policy that withholdeth but tendetli to poverty.

I shall require to take only a few moments, Mr. Speaker, to prove that the hon. gentleman is giving us to-night an exhibition of the complete reversal of all tire doctrines he preached in opposition. He tells us now that true economy consists in a large expenditure of money. Was that the doctrine of the Liberal party before 1896? Why, according to that party then, every dollar expended by the Conservative government of that day was wasted. The hon. gentleman opened his speech by telling us that certain predictions were made as to what
would happen the country if the Liberal party came into power. Let me ask him if the Liberal party had carried out their policy, would thes a predictions not have come true ? He knows that the only reasons these predictions were not fulfilled was because the government went hack on their tariff policy. Not one of the pledges they made did they fulfil, and these hon. gentlemen, now, with their usual modesty, boast that they have not fulfilled them. The hon. gentleman has told us that liberal expenditure is true economy.
Wise economy.	*

Well, I will accept the qualification which the hon. gentleman now makes. In 1896, when this government took office our expenditure was $44,334,000 aud it now is $62,084,000. What is there to show in the country for that expenditure ? What great public work has been constructed ? What is there to show for this immense jump from $44,000,000 in 1896 to $62,000,000. I challenge the hon. gentleman to point to anything which stands out prominently as an asset to Canada for that large amount of money. He cannot do it. The money lias been dribbled away in a wasteful manner in making works that are practically of no benefit to Canada.
1 come now to the crucial point in the bon. gentleman's speech, the only strong point, it seems to me, the only other point requiring an answer. He stated and restated that the Conservatives bad spent more than they had received, while the Liberals were justified in doing all they bad, because they spent less than they received. Am I right in so interpreting the hon. gentleman's speech ?
And I gave the figures for it. [DOT]

Yes, and I will give the hon. gentleman the figures now. The year 1898 was the first year when the hon. gentleman claimed a surplus. The receipts for that year were $40,556,510, and the expenditure was $45,334,281, or $4,777,771 more than the receipts.
My hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) knows that he is including the capital expenditure.
Certainly.

The ban. member for Pictori complained that we were charging too much to capital. In my remarks I made a clear distinction, and where the expenditure was on consolidated fund account, I said so.	[DOT]

That makes no difference. I am giving the total receipts and total expenditure. Let us not deceive ourselves or the country. The figures I have given show that, in 1898, when the hon. gentleman

claimed a surplus of $1,722,000 in round numbers, be bad actually spent $4,777,771 more than be bad received. 1 am taking the accounts as they are kept in England, in the United States-in fact in every civilized country except Canada. Now take the next year, in which the bon. gentleman said, be bad spent only 95 per cent of the whole income. As a matter of fact, be bad spent about four and three-quarter millions more than be had received. The income was $46,743,000, and the expenditure $51,542,000, or an excess of expenditure over receipts of $4,799,000. In 1900, the income of the Dominion of Canada was $51,031,000, and the expenditure $52,717,000, or an excess of expenditure over receipts of $1,186,000. Now in 1901 the receipts were $52,510,332, and the payments, $57,982,800, or an excess of expenditure of $5,406,000. Again, in 1902, the expenditure was $58,052,000 and the payments were $03,970,000-payments $5,918,000 more than the receipts. Yet the bon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fielding) rises here and cooly and blandly tells the House and the country that during these years he spent less than he received. Does the bon. gentleman adhere to that statement ?
The bon. gentleman asks a question I have no hesitation in answering. I gave the figures with regard to the late government and the present government on precisely the same basis.

For the purpose of what I am now saying, it is not necessary to compare the present government with the former one. I am taking the hon. gentleman on his own statement with regard to the receipts and expenditures of the whole of Canada, and I tell him that in the year when he says he spent 95 per cent of the whole income, he speqt four and three-quarter millions more than he received. The hon. gentleman cannot shelter himself behind the fact that he can take any sum he pleases and charge it up to capital account, and so declare a surplus of as many millions as he thinks will suit him. Will the hon. gentleman claim a surplus now for the period from 1897 to 1902 ? I am leaving out the last year, because I wish to deal with that separately. The hon. gentleman has claimed surpluses during that period to the amount of $27,971,000. To be perfectly fair, I am going to take the sinking fund that was applied on the public debt, although that was a statutory expenditure, and one made by former governments as well as by this one. If we take the six years before the present year, we find that the present government has paid about $14,000,000 to the sinking fund, while the former government paid something over $12,000,000. If we deduct the amount paid by this government on sinking fund, $14,459,000, during these years, from the total surpluses of the years, $27,791,000, there is still the sum of $13,331,000 to be accounted for. Now let me ask the hon.

gentleman what has become of that surplus ? I think this would be a very proper time for him to account for it. On a former occasion I asked the hon. gentleman the same question, and now I ask him again. What lias become of that money ?

I am surprised that the hon. gentleman should ask me to explain a thing that is so easily understood. Each and every one of these surpluses was applied to the capital account, and so, to that amount, additions which otherwise would have been made to the debt were abolished.

Ah ! Now we have the solution. The hon. gentleman charged it up to capital account-that was a piece of book-keeping. But that did not prevent the increase of the public debt, so the hon. gentleman had no surplus at all. For the first time the hon. gentleman has made perfectly clear the fraud that has been perpetrated on the people in declaring these surpluses. Well, he lias a surplus for the year 1903, not of $14,320,000, as he claimed, but of $4,949,770. His receipts for the year were $66,034,000, and his expenditure $02,084,000. These are the figures, yet the hon. gentleman declares that he has a surplus of $14,000,000. Will not the little boys In the schools laugh?
I think they will.

They will laugh-and if they do not laugh they will sneer-at calculation which shows receipts of $66,000,000, expenditures of $62,000,000, and a surplus of receipts over expenditures of $14,326,000. Is it not about time that we put an end to that sort of farce ? Is it not about time that we should tell the tax-payers the whole truth ? Is it not about time we should cease to make appologies like that of the hon. gentleman, telling the people that there are surpluses, when, as a matter of fact, the expenditure exceeds the income ? I challenge the hon. gentleman to say that except the year that 'has just closed, that during the whole period the Liberal party has been in power, there has been a single year in which the expenditure did not exceed the receipts. Yet the hon. gentleman gives as a sole justification of the large expenditure of this country, that his receipts were larger than the expenditure. I have no hesitation in saying that he is practising deception on the people of this country. It is not a fair statement, and it is not an accurate statement. I challenge the hon. gentleman now to deny that during the period from 1897 to 1902 there was a single year in which the hon. gentleman did not expend a sum in excess of that received, and that during these years the excess did not aggregate $27,791,281. Yet that was the sole excuse the hon. gentleman gives for the increased expenditure. Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to say a word about the Public Accounts Committee. The

lion, gentleman said that the Public Accounts Committee had become a farce.
The MINISTER OB' FINANCE. Not the Public Accounts, but the committee.

Well, the Public Accounts Committee of which the hon. gentleman was a distinguished member, became a farce, he says. Well, I am forced to agree that that is to some extent true. I know of more than one occasion on which that hon. gentleman turned it into a farce ; I know of occasions on which the hon. gentleman did not go there to assist the Public Accounts Committee in unravelling and detecting the wrongs that were committed under the government, but he went there to block the way, and by every means in his power to prevent an examination of that character. I remind him of one case when a witessi was asked to state the truth with regard to an account, and the Finance Minister was the first to come to his assistance and tell the witness that he need not answer the question. The hon. gentleman knows the case I refer to.
Will the hon. gentleman state the case ?

It was the case of Mr. Rochester, when he was asked what sums of money he paid out other than appeared in his accounts. If he had answered that question there would have been no trouble in putting our finger upon the raid that had been made upon the public treasury. The Minister of Finance was the first to rise in the Public Accounts Committee and to tell that witness that he need not answer the question. Yet the hon. gentleman comes here and says that the Public Accounts Committee is a farce.
The MINISTER OB' FINANCE. Does the hon. gentleman not know that that incident- which he has not described I think correctly-had relation to his friend the ex-Minister of Public Works that he now takes to his bosom, and that it occurred a year ago, not in the recent committees which are referred to ?
Well, if the hon. gentleman means to insinuate that there was something wrong on the part of the ex-Minister of Public Works
No. I do not.
Then why does the hon. gentleman refer to it ?
I refer to it because it happened to be a fact.

Then it must have some meaning. I am not denying that it was a case in which the department of the exMinister of Public Works was concerned. The hon. gentleman is making reference to it now with the evident intent of casting some blame upon the ex-Minister of Public Works.
No.
Then his reference has no meaning. Was he honest then when he told the witness not to answer the question ?

I am not casting any reflection on the ex-Minister of Public Works. The hon. gentleman was casting a reflection upon him and I was defending him from what I thought was an aspersion. But all that was a matter of a year ago, and my remarks had reference to the Public Accounts Committee of the present session.

Well, now, the hon. gentleman wants to make the short memory plea.
I am not dealing alone with the Public Accounts Committee of the present year. I think the hon. gentleman might have taken in past! years. But let us look at the present year. This has been a busy session, there has been no time to give to the Public Accounts Committee, or very little. But what has been disclosed in that committee that the hon. gentleman calls a farce ? I wish the member for West Middlesex (Mr. Calvert) was in his place. What was disclosed there only a. few days ago is a fair sample of the waste of public money that has gone on in this country with regard to the census. Why, Sir, one of the commissioners that was appointed by hon. gentlemen opposite, came down here and was examined before the Public Accounts Committee, and what was he forced to tell ? He was forced to tell in every case where a man had put in an account that he never questioned it, but still he paid it. He was forced to admit that they had hired horses in little villages of 200 or 300 inhabitants to drive the enumerators around for the purpose of taking the census when everybody knows that there was no horse hire, everybody knows that, it was a stuffing of the accounts, everybody knows it was a pillaging of the public treasury, yet the hon. gentleman says the committee was a farce. That is only one case that was brought out where the public treasury was pillaged. I say, Mr. Speaker, that if time had permitted ns to go into a large range of the public expenditures of this country, we would have discovered a great many cases of which the one I have just mentioned was only a sample. But there was not time, and the only case that we did examine was of the most frightful character ever disclosed before the Public Accounts Committee of this country.
Now, Sir, it is very amusing to see the hon. gentleman set up a defence of that kind. He says, we have been taunted about the Fast Atlantic Service, we are told by hon. members of the opposition that we should have a Fast Atlantic Service at any cost. Well, Sir, the hon. gentleman threw away the only opportunity we ever had in Canada to have a Fast Atlantic Service at a fair and moderate price. The hon. gentleman declared that the price was too high, and

bow they have lost the chance, and they are unable to get a service at twice as much as they could have got it for. Yet he taunts the opposition with saying that we are bound to have a service at any cost. This country does require a service, and if the hon. gentlemen threw away the opportunities, and if they have to pay double the cost of a service now, I would like to know with what propriety he can taunt this side with being willing to give twice as much as it could have been obtained for before. How is he going to answer for throwing away the opportunities that were given him, and of which he was an advocate for a number of years past ? The hon. gentleman threw away every chance they had of getting a service, so I do not think he takes the right position in blaming the opposition. Now, 1 want to call the hon. gentleman's attention 1o one matter on which he laid great stress : and I see the Minister of Customs sitting beside him who once made a similar chal-lege to the Conservative opposition. When we complain of the expenditure the Minister of Finance says :	Why don't you rise in
your place and move for a reduction. Did the Liberal party do anything of that kind during the 18 years they were in opposition ? During that whole period these able and vigilant gentlemen sat in this House. I see before me now one of them who never lost an opportunity of making a point against the government of the day, who is now an able minister and who was not particularly wanting in his duty in courage or in knowledge. During that whole period of 18 years $603,000,000 in round numbers were expended. Let me ask the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Paterson) how much of that was challenged during that whole period. Out of that sum of $603,000,000, but $447,000 was challenged. There were no votes against subsidies-not one. No hon. gentleman ever proposed to vote against a railway subsidy during that period. I think it is about time hon. gentlemen ceased making challenges of that kind. The Hon. Minister of Finance is unwittingly slandering the Hon. Minister of Customs because the hon. Minister of Customs was in the House before 1896 and was actively in opposition. I think I should come to the defence of those hon. gentlemen who were so derelict in their duty, who sat here while this country was being robbed, while $600,000,000 was being expended and who only had the courage to challenge a vote during that whole period in respect of less than half a million dollars. Now, I wish to say a word in regard to the prosperity of the country upon which the hon. minister has laid very great stress. He has told us what lias been done for the country. He says that we have expended money for the purpose of facilitating the business of Canada. I purpose to make a comparison in regard to agricultural products which is the main feature of our exports. It will be seen that we stand exact-Mr. CLANCY.
Iy in the same relative position that we occupied in 1896. I challenge the hon. gentleman to deny the fact. In 1896 Great Britain imported horses, cattle, sheep, bacon, hams, beef, mutton, pork, meats all other, lard, poultry and game, butter, cheese, milk condensed, &c., margarine, eggs, hides raw, sheep pelts, tallow, bristles, wool, wheat, barley, oats, pease, beans, corn, flour wheat, oatmeal, corn meal, grain and meal other, seeds, clover and grass, flax seed, hops, apples, cherries, grapes, pears, plums, other fruits, onions, potatoes, tomatoes, other vegetables, oil seed cake, flax, and fish. The total imports into the United Kingdom of these articles were $827,352,902. This of course includes fish. During that period Canada exported to Great Britain $53,254,758 or 6'43 per cent. Taking the total imports of the same articles of animal produce into the United Kingdom, the value in 1901 was $976,582,901. Of .this value the total amount imported from Canada was $66,446,101 or 6-SO per cent or less than 1 of 1 per cent of an increase during that period. Notwithstanding this vast expenditure of money we stand relatively in the same position as in 1896. But the hon. gentleman opposite to-night stated that the people were so prosperous that they have not only produced a great deal but that they have largely imported. The fact of the matter is, as the hon. gentleman knows, that the people of Canada have imported a large number of articles which they should have produced. They have been consuming foreign goods and there is not much in the boast that we have largely increased our import of goods which should have been produced under a proper policy in this country. I do not propose to pursue this subject any further than to say that we have an enormous expenditure, an alarming expenditure, which, as stated by my hon. friend from Pictou. represents no less a sum than $62,000,000 in round numbers. I challenge the hon. gentleman now In conclusion to put his finger upon one great service which is being performed and to show' wliat benefit Canada has from this increased expenditure. 1 say that it is impossible for the hon. gentleman tor his friends to show that as a result of this enormously increased expenditure, nearly double what it was in 1896, anything lias been done for the people that will stand to the credit of the government or that will confer some lasting benefit upon the country. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that the expenditure has been dribbled out for. the most useless purposes and that Canada has been called upon to pay immense sums for no substantial purpose. Just look at the sum which the taxpayer Iras to pay at the present time and w'liich he had to pay in 1896. The taxpayer had to pay in 1896 $7.50 per head for each man, woman and child. In 1903 every man, woman and child lias to pay $12.30 or $4.73 per head more than was paid in 1896. I repeat again that there is

absolutely nothing to show by way of a return for this immense tax put upon the people of the country. Hon. gentlemen opposite may say that we did not challenge it. As has been stated by my hon. friend from Pictou the opposition cannot lengthen the session surely beyond what it is now by dividing the House. The best way to indicate dissent is for an lion, member upon his responsibility to stand in his place and condemn that expenditure. Hon. gentlemen opposite are not slow in quoting speeches against us. Hon. gentlemen, when they go to the country, do not require to have votes. They will say that Mr. so and So made this statement and that they are prepared to hold them to it. We have not complained that hou. gentlemen in the past did not give evidence of their opposition to expenditures because they did not divide the House. It was they who raised the question and not we. I have nothing to say beyond this that we will leave it to the people of the country to decide they will have before them a set of promises from lion, gentlemen opposite and a set of performances that would not do much credit to any government even of less pretensions.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to detain the House long but I want to refer to one case to show the reason why the Public Accounts Committee may have been somewhat of a farce.
I refer to the case of an individual who is acting as private secretary for Mr. Charle-son. What are the facts in connection with the conduct of this man whose name is Gobeil. The Auditor General reports that he refuses to give any vouchers for his expenditure. At page 333-323 of the Auditor General's Report for 1900, we And that this man sent $2,809.93 for sundries, supplies, &c., and that he absolutely refused to produce any vouchers. Why is this private secretary whose salary was raised from $700 a year to $2,400 without any examination, why is he allowed to go about the country and spend his time at Syracuse, N. Y., and elsewhere, and have his expenses paid by the government 1 What is he doing there for Mr. Ckarleson ? In the Auditor Gen eral's Report for the year ending 30th June, 1899, the Auditor General complains that this private secretary is allowed to break all the rules governing his case. He goes to Vancouver or wherever he likes, he spends all the money he likes, and he produces no vouchers. And yet. the Minister of Finance talks about the Public Accounts Committee being a farce. Of course it is a farce; what is the use of having a fire without wood; what is the use of having an investigation without vouchers ? The government want it to be a farce, and the greater farce it is the better they are pleased. Why is it that the private secretary of a contractor, paid out of the people's money, is allowed to go wherever he likes, and allowed to refuse giving vouchers ?
Does he go to Syracuse for the good of his health, or for the good of the health of some hon. gentlemen connected with the department ? It would not be healthy to have him here while the Public Accounts Committee is in session. There is not the slightest doubt that the Minister of Public Works, who is not now in the House, but who ought to be, knows very well for whose health this man goes to Syracuse. This government does not want vouchers to be produced; they have a horror of them.

Consolidation of Dominion statutes, whioh may be paid notwithstanding anything contained in the Civil Service Act or in the Act respecting the Department of Public Printing and Stationery, $16,000.
Who are the commissioners ?

I gave the names of the commissioners a few days ago when this matter was up in another form. The commissioners are : Mr. New-combe, the Deputy Minister of Justice ; Mr. Power, another employee of the Department of Justice ; Mr. Cameron, Registrar of the Supreme Court; Sir Henry Strong, ex-Chief Justice of the Supreme Court ; Mr. Sirois, of Quebec; Mr. Roscoe, and Mr. St. Louis, secretary of the commission, the names of the others were given on a previous occasion.
How much is it expected that the revision will cost ?

It is very hard to say; the last revision took place in 1886, and cost, if I remember rightly, somewhere in the neighbourhood of $48,000. We have, up to the present, expended in connection with this consolidation the sum of
$16,000. We expect to keep within the $48,000, notwithstanding the fact that we have to revise the statutes from 1886 down to the present time, 17 years. That vote of $20,000 has been in the estimates for the last four or five years. In 1902-3 we expended $12,722.38; in 1903-4 we expended $3,398.71, so that the total expenditure up to the present time is $16,121.09.
How far has the work advanced and wbat now remains to be done ?

I am now speaking from memory, and my hon. friend will find that I gave all of these details and that they are on ' Hansard.' My recollection is that there are about 154 statutes to be revised, and of that number 17 have been completely revised and 38 have been prepared and are ready now to lie passed upon. They are partially revised, and the i whole work is expected to be completed next year.
Why should it cost over $40,000 to revise 150 statutes ?
I estimate that it will cost $40,000 odd, because the revision of 1886 cost $48,000.
We must do better than this.
We will do better than this.

I do not think that is a fair comparison, because you have now as a basis the Revised Statutes of 1886. That was the first revision and it naturally took a long time. I think that more than 150 statutes were revised in 1886.
I do not remember the exact number; at all events, this is equally important and equally expensive with the work done in 1886, if not more so. There are now seventeen years of statutes to be revised.

In the other case there were 20 years of statutes to be revised, and that was the first revision; a great many of the statutes that are now being revised are mere amendments to particular chapters of the revised statutes. I think the work, while equally important, would be less laborious and would occupy less time than the work of 1886.
Galops rapids-to complete channel. $60,000.

This matter was discussed on a previous occasion. It is for some improvements in the Galops rapids, where we have spent a vast sum of money. One hon. member in this House expresssed the opinion that this was not a useful work, but the view taken by the department is that it is useful, and it does seem a pity that for the small sum still required we should abandon the work. We have spent $978,000 to improve the
Galops rapids, and we are advised that this hon. minister to make a note of this, and will complete the work.	another session bring in a vote for it.
Is any record kept in the department of the number of vessels using this channel ? I am inclined to think it is neglected and not used at all.

We have no record of vessels using it, but we have a report from the engineer of the department in charge of the St. Lawrence, who thinks it is very important that we should finish up the work by making this expenditure.
Trent canal-construction. $360,000.
This is to complete the work of construction on the different sections, comprising sections 2 and 3, and also the steel work for the hydraulic lock on the Peterborough section.
Are there any new contracts this year ?
No, but very considerable operations are still going on.
What is the report of the engineer on Lhe feasibility of connecting Rice lake and Port Hope instead of going down to Trenton ?

I shall be glad to furnish the report. It is in substance favourable to the Trenton section rather than Port Hope. I shall see that the hon. member for East Durham (Mr. Ward) has access to it.
