1 would ask the hon. minister if he has any report about opening up the waters north of Balsam lake ? I do not know of any part of Canada which would derive equal benefit from an expenditure of $100,000. Such an expenditure would open up 100 miles of waterway, by building four or five locks north of Balsam lake. We have voted cheerfully large sums for building docks, bonusing railways, to mills and all that sort of thing in the maritime provinces and the province of Quebec, but I do not know of any part of the Dominion, in which so large an area would be so materially benefited by the expenditure of this sum, as would the counties of Victoria and Haliburton by the construction of four or five small locks, at the outside seventy-five feet. I would ask the
What depth would you get ?

In the river there is lots of water. Five feet in the canal would be plenty. All we want is to get boats in and out to move down the cribs of hardwood timber. There would also be a tourist passenger traffic in that district. At the same time, I would ask him to make a note of this fact. The system of opening and closing those locks is not the most modern. The superintendent says they are improving the system, but at present it is very tedious.
Which locks ?

All the locks along the entire system. In the old days the Trent canal was rather pooh-poohed, but I am glad to see that the hon. gentleman from Ontario is a strong advocate of it today. He will find that Lake Skugog, that large lake in his own town, will be immensely benefited when this lock is opened up. I am glad to see that he is a strong supporter of the construction of 'this work.
Railways and Canals'-chargeable to capital-Ratlways-Intercolonial-to dredge and ballast rock at deep water terminus at Halifax, $25,000.
The! MINISTER OF FINANCE. This is made necessary by the increasing draft of the steamers. There is a good wharf there, and what used to be a good depth of water. But with the increasing size of the Allan steamers it is necessary to dredge to a depth of 30 feet.
National Transcontinental Railway-to provide for surveys and other expenses, $500,000.

This is the first installment of the expenditure on the government's portion of the new railway. This amount is designed to cover only incidental expenses and surveys. Of course, there will be no work in construction until the House meets again. In the meantime it is intended to organize and send out survey parties.
I see by the Montreal ' Star ' of this evening that Mr. Hays says he has survey parties all over the road. Is the government paying for these ?

No arrangement has been made with respect to that. But if the Grand Trunk have made surveys which can be properly utilized, I tfiink we should be glad to have the work advanced to that extent and to utilize the result. And if we utilize the work of the surveys, no doubt some arrangement will be made to bear our fair share of the expense.
The government have not selected the commissioners or the chief engineer ?
Has the hon. minister that estimate here ? When does he propose commencing work ?

Of course, construction cannot be commenced until we have the survey. I suppose that immediately after the enactment of the measure steps will be taken to push the surveys forward. No doubt something can be done this autumn and winter to make provision for numerous surveys. Whatever can be done will be pushed forward with all speed.
Are the surveys below Quebec sent out by the government or by the Grand Trunk Pacific?
They will be sent out on behalf of the government through the instrumentality of the commissioners.
I understood the hon. gentleman to say there were some there already.
Some between Winnipeg and Quebec. I am not aware that any have been sent out by the Grand Trunk east of Quebec.
I would like to see the estimate to which the hon. gentleman referred, to see how the work is to be divided. Of course, if this were a small sum I would not ask it.

The deputy minister in his estimate has not designated any particular points where the parties will be established. But he has estimated that twenty parties could be usefully employed between Winnipeg and Moncton- fourteen between Winnipeg and Quebec and six between Quebec and Moncton. He has not designated the places where they will commence work.
But it must be divided into sections.
Yes, the work will be arranged by sections under the chief engineer, just like any other railway work, and a large number of parties will be put in the field to push the work with all speed.
When will the work of survey begin ?
As soon as we can have the surveyors appointed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is every disposition to push the work. I should think that immediately after the session parties will be put in the field and the work proceeded with as long as the season will permit.
The Montreal ' Star' says :

Hays, general manager and second vice-president of the Grand Trunk Railway, has made the following statement regarding the company's plans for completing the Grand Trunk Pacific :-
The reconnaisance survey is proceeding vigorously and, in fact, has been, ever since early last spring. We have between fifteen and twenty parties in the field, some of whom have about completed the work of their division ; others will keep on all through the winter. Great care has been taken with a view of obtaining a line with a minimum grade, not exceeding 4 per cent

I presume that means 4-10ths per cent.
-or twenty feet to the mile, about the same as the maximum grade between Toronto and Montreal, and with ho greater than two or three degree curves.
On some portions of the route where the country is comparatively unknown', for instance, in- the Lake Nepigon district, owing to the lack of transportation facilities, supplies are difficult to obtain, and progress is not as great as otherwise would be the case.
Plans for construction at' the point at which a beginning will he made are dependent on the completion of surveys. We have now the territory pretty well covered. The first parties we sent out, which were started before the government policy as to the eastern division was developed, were located between Winnipeg and North Bay, the theory being that that was the section of country that was most in need of additional facilities, and while it is undoubtedly true that, for some years to come, a large proportion of the grain crop of the North-west will move out by water during the season of navigation, there is to-day a very considerable quantity moving by rail north of Lake Superior and this quantity will be increased in a constantly growing volume as rail facilities for the economical and expeditious movement of the traffic are provided. The new line with its 4 per cent grade

Meaning, no -doubt, 4-10ths per -cent.
-will- have great advantages in this respect.
Our surveying parties are also well distributed across the territory from Winnipeg west and construction on that portion of the line will he pushed as soon as the results of our surveys are known, as also the construction of the branches from a port on Lake Superior (which port is yet to be determined) to a junction with the eastern division and a line from North Bay, north also to intersect the eastern division.
As to plans and intentions in connection with the work on the eastern division, I shall have to refer you to the government, that portion of the undertaking being, as you are aware, under their control.
While it is dependent on conditions generally, the results of surveys, the situation as regards labour, movement of supplies, material, &c., it is not likely that the road will be completed short of five years.
So it would seem that the Grand Trunk Pacific are surveying the line to the north. This is a nice little piece of campaign literature, and X thought I would read it for the benefit of the minister.
On which side ?	-

Well, turn it either way. What I want to know is whether the -government will instruct the chief engineer, when they appoint him, to take over these survey parties ? I understand that they are almost entirely American.

We have no arrangement with the Grand Trunk in that respect. I understand their surveys are between North Bay and Winnipeg. Of course, only that part of their line which coincides with the contemplated line of the government can be used. But if bona fide surveys have been made which are found useful for the government's purposes, I think we should take them over and make a fair allowance for them.
And take over the engineers, too ?
Not necessarily, but take over the surveys. However, this is speculative, as we have no arrangement.

Does the hon. gentleman intend, when lie appoints survey parties, that they shall enter upon the ground already surveyed by the Grand Trunk ? The hon. gentleman has just said that if a portion of these surveys turned out to be valuable the Grand Trunk people would be recouped for their outlay. That does not seem. unreasonable, unless the hon. gentleman intends to put a staff over the same territory.

I think where competent engineers have covered the ground to the satisfaction of the chief engineer, after his appointment, I would not suppose it necessary to go over the same ground. That would be a matter in which we would take the advice of the chief engineer. After allowing for the work which the Grand Trunk have begun, there is still a large amount of work to be done which will require a number of parties. The estimate is made for the whole section. If it turns out that the Grand Trunk have completed the surveys for a reasonable distance, we would use a portion of this money to pay them for their surveys instead of organizing independent surveys.
Does the sum now asked for cover the whole cost of the surveys between Winnipeg and Moncton ?

This estimate we think will be the cost of operations within the present year. I do not know that
it will cover the whole cost of the surveys,
I should think not.
Has the hon. gentleman any idea as to what they will cost ?
They will cost very much more than that. These are the estimates for the first year's operations..
I suppose if the Grand Trunk Pacific Company had made some surveys the hon. gentleman would be in possession of that information.

We know they have made some surveys, but how far they may be adapted to the government's purpose and how far they relate to branches which belong to the Grand Trunk proper, will he a matter for investigation.
How much is allotted to each party of surveyors ?
About $30,000 or $31,000 for each party for the year. But as a portion of this year is already past we are not taking a full year's appr. priation.
When will they begin operations ? I understand that these operations can be carried on during the winter.

Yes, so far as the season will permit. They will begin immediately. After the passing of the legislation I presume the government will take the necessary steps to give effect to the intention of parliament. We desire to get the surveyors into the field with the least possible delay.
How many are employed in each party ?
The chief engineer has made a report to me, but I have not it at hand. If my hon. friend wishes for the information before concurrence, I will get it to-morrow.
Is there a staff out already ?
Not on behalf of the government. The Grand Trunk people, according to current report, have some surveyors at work. But there has been no work on behalf of the government yet.
Have you any report from any staff working at present on these surveys ?
No, we have no such reports. We have no communication with them on.the subject whatever.

I noticed some time ago that a gentleman by the name of McGinnis, of the Geological Survey, returned home, and I saw interviews from some of the men who had been in his party,

and one of them said that for upwards of 100 miles where this road was going, there was nothing but muskegs. Has the minister heard anything about it ?

No.

Soulanges canal-to pay J. & M. O'Leary interest on $17,467.28, from March 1, 1900, to August 28, 1903, at 5 per cent, $3,050.79.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Why was that not settled before ?

This claim has only recently been paid, although the work was done some time ago. The final estimates were not made up for a considerable time. The principal sum had been paid to them, and we are now proposing to pay them interest from the date at which it should begin, at five per cent. Where we pay interest at all I think there is much to he said in favour of taking the standard rate. Interest is a matter of grace, and we may not pay it at all, but in a case where these contractors have to borrow money from the banks, it is not unreasonable that they should be allowed five per cent for any delay on the part of the government.
Is there any revenue received from the lease of water-power ?
Yes, the deputy thinks it is about $3,000 a year.

Elections-to pay the account of the Prince Albert ' Advocate ' for advertising the proclamation and notice- of the Saskatchewan election of 1900, notwithstanding anything in the Dominion Elections Act, $297.48.

This item is inserted at the request of the Auditor General who became satisfied that the charge is a fair one, but he is not certain that he has the authority to pay it and he therefore asks for a vote of the House.
How does it come that there is an item of $297 in connection with this election and nothing at all in connection with any other election in the west ?
This was ordered without authority ?

Yes, I am told it has been the custom to publish this advertisement and that it has been paid for on a previous occasion. The returning officer in his report says :
It bias always been customary here (Saskatchewan) to publish proclamations and election notices in both English -and French. The reason for this is the territory is so large and many settlers so isolated that it is impossible to cover -the district thoroughly with postal notices of proclamation. If it were not for the circulation of newspapers undoubtedly many persons would be in ignorance on election day as to where they should vote or would have great inconvenience in finding out. ... As an aid in distributing this information as it should be distributed the newspaper is invaluable and the necessity of its use is beyond question.
Did the Conservative paper not get the advertisement too ?
I do not know whether this is a Conservative or a Liberal paper.

Why did the Conservative paper not get it ? I am surprised at the hon. minister pressing a matter of this kind. I hope that in future he will see that the Tory papers get it so that the poor Tories will know where to go and vote. Will the hon. Minister of Finance make a promise to that effect 1
That will be taken into consideration.
What amount was paid in the general elections in 1896 ?
I cannot give the hon. gentleman the amount, but I am informed by one of my officers that he has discussed the matter with the Auditor General and he says it was1 paid on a previous occasion.
Was it paid by a special vote ?
At that time it was paid without a special vote, but the Auditor General has become a little more critical and he likes to have votes.
This is to help the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) In his next election, I suppose ?

It seems to me that the returning officer has neglected his duty. Surely a notice In a newspaper is not the notice to be given to the electors by proclamation. There seems to be an irregularity in that explanation. It would appear that the returning officer did not post up the proclamations in order to give the people notice of the election, but that he paid the newspaper to do his duty.
AVhat I would understand from the information furnished is that the legal notices were given, but that they would be insufficient and that they were supplemented by this newspaper advertisement.
In the dual language ?
I presume so.

I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Finance if he intends to take up any items that have been passed in connection with the Post Office Department ? The reason I ask is that there is an item standing which the lion. Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock) was to give some information about. It will not take much discussion.
What was that ?
In regard to a post office in the west. The hon. Postmaster General was to bring down certain petitions and letters in connection with it.

If the hon. Postmaster General promised my hon. friend that certain information would be brought down I will see that he gets it, so as to have an opportunity of discussing it whether it is on this item or any other.
We did not get an explanation as to why it is necessary to publish the proclamation in this special newspaper in all western Canada and not necessary to do the same thing in any other constituency.

I noticed the other night when this matter was under discussion that the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) said that he recognized that the conditions of Saskatchewan were exceptional and that it might be quite reasonable and necessary to publish the notice there and not necessary elsewhere owing to the territory being so large and the difficulty of distributing the notices.

The hon. minister should not add insult to injury by trying to stuff the committee. There is no reason for any such explanation. If the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) had stated that
in his own constituency that there was some need for this same thiug there would be some sense in it. In Saskatchewan there is no settlement east of Prince Albert, settlement to the north only extends for 21 miles aud south and west this paper will not circulate. The hon. minister's explanation was that these poor people would not know where to go and vote but for the publication of this notice. If it is necessary to tell the Liberals how to vote, and I admit that they require a little more information than the Conservatives do, I insist that the Conservatives should also have an opportunity of knowing where to vote. Do I understand my hon. friend to promise that if one paper gets it next year the other paper will also get it ?
I may not have control of it next year.
Will ihe hon. minister give it serious consideration ?
Yes, I will agree to that.

The minister states that a similar amount to this was paid in 1896.
The -MINISTER OF FINANCE. I am informed by one of my officers that he learned from the Auditor General that an amount for the same purpose was paid after the general election of 1896.
Why did the Auditor General pay the amount in 1896 without a special vote of parliament, and why does he require a special vote now ?
There are a number of things which the Auditor General has been doing for years, the legality of which he now questions, and asks that they be done in a different way.
He is getting suspicious.
Perhaps so ; he has written a letter asking that this vote be taken for the reason that the Election Act does not sanction this method of publication.
Does the hon. gentleman know what is the circulation of this paper, or does he know if it was done without the instruction of the returning officer ?

It is evident that the returning officer authorized it, judging from a reference in the letter of the Auditor General, who asks us to be good enough to include the amount in the supplementary estimates for the present fiscal year.	*

The Auditor General asks for this vote.
To provide for expenses of investigation into trade combinations. Customs tariff Act, $5,000.

This is to provide for any investigations which may be held under this Act. Mr. Justice Rich-

ards is now inquiring into tile alleged lumber combine in Manitoba. We have bad no report yet.
Contribution by Canada to Queen Victoria memorial, $146,000.

This is an appropriation which the ministers in London last year agreed with Mr. Chamberlain to recommend to the consideration of parliament, as a contribution to the national memorial to the late Queen. The different colonies of the empire have, I think, all contributed, and the ministers agreed to recommend to the Canadian parliament a vote of 130,000 sterling. This memorial is to be erected in London, near Buckingham palace. The idea is that the memorial shall include designs to represent the various portions of the empire, but it is not advanced far enough at present to go into details.

Carried.
To pay Charles Miller $3,713.32 and Robert Miller $3,339.05 for amounts deposited by them in the post office savings bank at St. Scholas-tique and fraudulently withdrawn by the assistant postmaster, $7,052.37.
This item stood over for some information. If there were any other depositors who lost money why were they not paid 7
These are the only persons who lost money.
One of the questions asked was that the principal and interest should be separated. It arose on the question of how large a sum might be deposited at one time.
I find on inquiry from file superintendent of the savings bank that the rules admit of a deposit of $3,000 at one time.
There was also a point about the insurance fund. Would the hon. minister give us a statement in respect to the amount paid out of this fund and how the fund stands at the present moment ?

Bonds are taken only from postmasters and not from subordinates. The person who did this embezzling was an employee of the postmaster. It has never been the practice of the department to require bonds or security from the subordinate officials in an office of this kind.
Were there no bonds to be attached and was there no responsibility nesting u?on the postmaster ?

The Dostmaster himself gives bonds but the bonds taken from a postmaster at an office where, the revenue is not very large are small in amount and quite inadequate to meet any loss that might happen. The postmaster himself has given bonds of a private character. This was an old appointment not Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
occurring under our administration or under the modern system of security by assessment. Nothing has been recovered on it and it, is not thought that anything will be recovered from the postmaster.
Do I understand that the postmaster appointed had bonds that were of no value to the department ? Are we to understand that the department were so, shall I say-
Say anything you like ; make it good and strong.

My hon. friend I hope is not inviting special criticism. The statement he has now given to the committee is different from the statement which he made the other day.
The POSTMASTER GENERAL I said that the general system adopted in the department to-day was to insure by the system of assessment and that I was under the impression that it was probable that this deputy postmaster was insured under that assessment system. On inquiry I find that the postmaster was an old officer who had given his security before the assessment system was adopted.
What steps were taken to find out whether these bonds were valueless or to recover from the sureties ?
I do not know what steps were taken to recover : the Deputy Postmaster General states that nothing has been recovered.
Are we to understand that bonds are taken from a postmaster and not from a deputy postmaster ?	.

The system is to take bonds from the postmaster. We have not an arbitrary rule although I encourage, and favour the assessment system in preference to the private bond system. When the hon. gentleman is in a responsible position in a government, he will find that it is not always so easy to recover from private sureties. I have endeavoured to have the assessment system adopted in all new appointments, although even in the case of new appointments an option is given to the postmasters where the amount of security is comparatively trifling.

Might I ask the minister what system he has of investigating and examining into the value of bonds given by postmasters in such a case as this. There seems to have been slackness on the part of the hon. gentleman.

No doubt the department took all the proper business steps to find out whether the bondholders were good or not. I presume that an inquiry was made by the inspector of the district. The bond was taken by our predecessors, and no doubt at that time the

sureties made the usual affidavit of justification and the bond was assumed to be of good value. But when you try to recover on a bond, you will find it frequently impossible to get anything. Sometimes sureties will swear to their solvency, and yet when a loss occurs you cannot recover. Moreover people's conditions alter.
Was there a law suit in this case ?
What does the hon. gentleman mean ?
What steps did the department take to recover the sum of $7,000 which we are asked to vote ?
I did not say that the bonds were for $7,000. I am quite satisfied that they were for no such sum.
Nor did I say they were, but I am asking the hon. gentleman to state what steps were taken to recover from the bondsmen who went security to the amount of the loss.

My hon. friend has misunderstood me. I did not say that there were bonds for $7,000. It is not the practice to exact security to that extent, and I have no doubt that in this case there was no departure from the rule and that the amount of the bond was comparatively small as compared with the loss. My officer informed me that nothing could be recovered and I did not see what could be gained by a suit. As to the real embezzler, he has no means, but his family are very well off, and it was thought at one time that they would, for the honour of the family, come forward and make some contribution. However, they have not done so.
Can the hon. gentleman give me the information I asked for with regard to the dismissal at Port Lambton of a postmistress ?

Are
we through with this estimate ?
If the hon. gentleman wishes to go on, I will not delay him.
Do I understand that it is within the power of any postmaster to name a deputy, and if that deputy has power to do all the work of the office and receive money on deposit and yet not give any bond V

The
postmaster must give security and he is responsible for the official he engages to assist him. Those he engage are sworn in by the inspector, who is supposed to exercise some discretion and in that way there is some departmental supervision as to who shall assist the postmaster. But the postmaster himself is the only one the govern-459
ment knows. In this case the postmaster gave a bond but the securities were not good for the amount, so that it was not considered possible to recover anything from them. Neither the sureties nor the postmaster are worth anything. The postmaster is responsible for the defalcation of his agent and his bond would cover that defalcation. It would not be practicable to obtain security from everybody engaged to work under the postmaster in a small post office. The emoluments of aniy of those1 postmasters are comparatively trifling and the value of the business trivial, and yet it would be possible for them to embezzle considerable sums. The postmasters are men of standing and character, which is the best security one can have, although one must not disregard ordinary business precautions and the taking of proper security.

I do not think that the hon. minister has given a satisfactory explanation. In the first place, under the rule bnly $3,000 can be deposited; but it seems that there were two depositors in this case and the amount was $7,000. How could $7,000 belonging to two individuals get into the hands of this deputy ?

The man who committed these frauds got possession of the pass books of the depositors. In one instance he received $2,000 or $3,000 and only transmitted to the department a portion of that money, so that the superintendent of the money order branch was not aware that an attempt was being made to deposit more than the regulations allowed. It was not known by the department that that amount of money had been delivered to this man until the defalcation was discovered in the fall of 1892. The embezzler altered the entry in the pass book, and for a long time retained possession of it. It was only when the depositor insisted in getting possession of the pass book and not getting it communicated with the superintendent of the savings bank at Ottawa that the frauds came to light.
The depositor must certainly have known that he was exceeding the legal limit of the deposit.
No, the difference was in the interest.
Then this thing must have lasted a long while to have accumulated all its interest.
It began in 1895 and lasted until 1902
Then for seven years this depositor never saw his pass book ?
I did not say that.
The moment he saw it 1 he must have known.
He was an illiterate man-could neither read nor write.
It seems strange that this could be carried on for seven years and nobody any the wiser. Would not the postmaster know what deposits were being made ?
This man was the assistant.
It seems that the postmaster might as well-
It was a postmistress.
Does the postmistress still retain her position ?
I do not think so, but am not sure.

The Postmaster General does not seem to know more than the law allows about this matter. Of course, the amount is not. very large, but this seems to be establishing a precedent, and the committee should have the facts so as to be able to judge whether the money should be voted or not. The information must be in the hon. gentleman's department, and the item was left over in order that he might inform himself. On the basis of the facts made known, it seems to me we are not legally bound to pay this money. There may be an equitable claim, and that, of course, we should recognize. But it seems to me that this assistant postmaster was simply the agent of the Millers. He was handling their money and investing it for them. Of course, he may have made a bad investment of a considerable portion. I suppose there were pass-books ?

Yes. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) was not present when I made the explanation before. The assistant postmaster received money to transmit, but did not transmit it all. In one instance, I think he received $3,000 and only deposited $1,000. Having the passbook of these men, I think he forged the amount in the deposit book, or falsified the entries. He threw the men off their guard and retained custody of the pass-book. Another method of, embezzlement was to forge the name of the depositor to applications for withdrawals, transmit the pass-book of which he had the custody, and, as it was easy to recognize tjie envelope in which it came, intercepted the pass-book when it was sent back addressed to the depositor. Then he would forge the endorsement on the cheques issued on the savings banks. I am not familiar with all the details, but the case was in the hands of the Minister of Justice.

He retained some of the money, $2,000. Then be Mr. FOWLER.
forged requisitions on the department and intercepted the cheques payable to the order of the Millers. Then he forged the endorsement of the Millers on the cheque, and so the money never legally left the custody of the government.
Did he take all the money ?
He took the whole business-simply left the books.
Would not the banks be responsible when he forged the endorsation V
There was the forged requisition in the first place.
The government issued a cheque on the forged requisition ?
The forgery of the endorsation would not make the government liable, but the forgery of the requisition.
Yes.
Perhaps the hon. Postmaster General would give me the information now on the item that was allowed to stand-the petitions and correspondence with regard to the Lambton post office.
I am sending to the hon. gentleman (Sir. Clancy) the papers he asked for.

I do not wish to delay the consideration of this item to go over these papers. Do I understand that there are in these papers, which the hon. gentleman sent me, all the petitions and letters that passed ?
I think that everythinig the hon. gentleman asked for is there.
I have a letter from the postmaster at Tatamagouche post office, in Colchester county, asking what is done with the money kept as a percentage from the postmasters.

If the officer at Tatamagouche is insured under the assessment system, his assessment goes into the common fund. There is an insurance fund that is deposited in the post office savings bank as an insurance fund, and in the event of a defalcation on the part of any officer so insured, the amount for which he is insured in the fund is withdrawable from the fund by Order in Council. It is the same as with a corporation that issues fidelity bonds. They accept premiums from those insured, and these premiums are the means wherewith the company carries on its business and makes its profits and meets its losses. I think in a place of this size the postmaster would give a bond of perhaps $400 at the outside.
Where can we find a report of that insurance fund ?

It is not entered in the public accounts, it is a trust fund. Under the Act there is a trust fund which is not handed over to the receiver general or to the Postmaster General, but it is deposited in the savings bank as a special trust fund to be drawn upon to meet any loss occasioned by the defalcation of an officer.
Is it in the report 1

There is no statement of that in the report. I could get a statement from the savings bank. We have an officer who looks after that in the books of the department.
Amount required for compensation for price of islands and improvements to be made on islands in the St. Lawrence river, $12,000.

The American authorities have several islands which have been kept as open parks with public landings. But there is no similar accommodation among the Canadian islands, and the purpose of this is to establish several public landings and to purchase sufficient grounds for the purpose, so that Canadians passing up and down may have some public landing places.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: This is in accordance with an arrangement entered into between the Department of Marine and Fisheries and the Department of Public Works, with a deputation from the United States several years ago. The American government purchased and set apart a number of islands at certain points for public parks, both for Canadians and for Americans, and the Canadian government agreed to do the same. The islands that are set apart by the Canadian government belong to the Indian Department, and the government must vote the money and place it to the credit of the Indian Department in order to acquire the lands. I am glad to see that the government have acted on this arrangement after several years.

Before the committee rises, I wish to ask the Minister of Finance with regard to a petition to retain a post office where it was in the first instance, and where it had been for years, in a building belonging to a man by the name of McNulty, who was then postmaster. I do not see that petition among the papers.

I brought down all the papers my hon. friend asked for. I told my deputy to go through the ' Hansard ' and see all that my hon. friend asked for, and transmit all the papers asked for. He says he has sent me more than the hon. gentleman asked for.

I asked for all the letters, papers and petitions in connection with it. I am not saying the hon. gentleman is withholding anything. I am merely asking if he has complied as far as possible with my request.
459i

I have here a memorandum from my deputy in which he tells me he has sent me all that the hon. gentleman asked for, if not more.
I have not looked at the ' Hansard ' to see what my hon. friend asked for, but if he will go through the ' Hansard ' he will find that what he asked for is there, or else my deputy has misinformed me.

I only wish to be sure that all that is in the department in connection with the matter has been brought down. Of course it may have been that the petition was not sent to the department, but I know it was intended to be sent.
I find there is one small item of $1,300 which has been omitted in the estimates, and I have procured the consent of His Excellency for the same.

speechtext:
The MINISTER OF PTNANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding) delivered a message from His Excellency the Governor General.
Mr. SPEAKER read the message as follows :
Minto.
The Governor General transmits to the House of Commons further supplementary _ estimates of sums required for the public service of the Dominion for the year ending 30th June, 1904, and, in accordance with the provisions of ' the British North America Act, 1867,' the Governor General recommends these estimates to the House of Commons.
Government House, Ottawa,
21st October, 1903.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved that the message of His Excellency together with the estimates be referred to the Committee of Supply.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext:
This is one of the judges of the province of Nova Scotia who has been laid aside by a very severe illness, and who is now about to retire. It has been agreed between himself and the government that for one year he shall be allowed his full salary. He is a comparatively young man who but for his illness would have many years of service on the bench. It has been agreed that the

government shall recommend the payment of his full salary for one year after which he will receive the ordinary superannuation.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE presented a report from the special committee appointed to draw up reasons to be offered at a conference with the Senate for disagreeing with certain amendments made by the Senate to Bill (No. 21) entitled an Act to amend and consolidate the law respecting Railways.

That a conference be desired with the Senate for the purpose of communicating the reasons which induce this House not to concur in the amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. (21) intituled : * An Act to amend and consolidate the law respecting railways.'
Motion agreed to.
That a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint their honours therewith.

Motion agreed to.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved the adjournment of the House.
What will be the order of business for to-morrow ?
The resolutions touching the Quebec bridge.

After that ?
The MINISTER OF1 FINANCE. Concurrence and any matters which remain on the paper generally.
